The proposals indicate that the UK ETS will be designed to ensure minimal differences for businesses in these sectors compared to operating under the EU ETS . <p> The UK ETS will be part of a broader policy framework to deliver the UK 's net zero target by 2050 , including a ? 2 billion fund to support decarbonisation in a range of sectors and the ? 315 million Industrial Energy Transformation Fund7 to support industry to invest in energy efficiency and decarbonisation technologies . <p> Next Steps <p> The Government must now present legislation to the Parliament at Westminster , the Scottish Parliament , the National Assembly in Wales , and the Assembly in Northern Ireland in 2020 , so that the UK ETS can be launched in January 2021 . <p> To view all formatting for this article ( eg , tables , footnotes ) @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 
@@42065008 <h> Brexit <p> Prime Minister Boris Johnson has based most of his campaign around Brexit ( Photo : Chris J Ratcliffe/Getty ) <h> Brexit process/timing <h> Conservatives <p> Leave the EU on 31 January with an 11-month transition period during which nothing will change . Immediately start talks on a free-trade agreement with the EU . Do not extend the transition under any circumstances , even if talks over a comprehensive trade deal with Europe break down . If necessary , leave the transition period without a trade agreement at the end of 2020 . <h> Labour <p> Immediately agree a further delay to the Article 50 process , pushing the default Brexit date past summer 2020 . Negotiate a new Withdrawal Agreement with the EU within three months , based on the original text agreed by Theresa May but with major changes to the attached political declaration . This would include a transition period of uncertain length . This Brexit deal would be put to a referendum against Remain . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Write to the president of the European Commission revoking the UK 's Article 50 notification within hours of a new government taking office . This would end the Brexit process altogether , with the UK staying in the EU indefinitely on the same terms as now . <h> Green Party <p> Quickly agree a delay to Article 50 to give time for a referendum on membership of the EU , which would be held as quickly as possible . <h> Brexit Party <p> Either leave without a deal on 31 January , or negotiate a delay of a few months in order to agree a standstill under the terms of " Gatt XXIV " -- this would see the UK and EU both agree to continue trading on the same terms as now while they hold talks on a comprehensive free-trade agreement laying out the permanent relationship . <h> Ukip <p> Leave the EU without any form of Withdrawal Agreement as soon as possible -- which would almost certainly mean 31 January . Deal with the EU on World Trade Organisation terms while discussing a free-trade deal . <h> SNP <p> The party is totally opposed to Brexit given that Scots votes by 62 per cent to Remain in 2016 , and its manifesto says voting SNP could provide an " escape from Brexit " through independence . It adds that there is " no way " that the process of exiting the EU will be completed in the next few months and will instead go on " for years " as trade negotiations commence . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Delay Article 50 immediately to hold a second referendum on Brexit in the first few months of 2019 . Work with other pro-Remain parties to achieve this . <h> Summary : <p> The quickest way to resolve the Brexit impasse is to revoke Article 50 immediately as the Lib Dems suggest . Next would be leaving on 31 January as currently scheduled , while holding a second referendum would extend the process by several months . No party admits the truth : that whether we Leave or Remain , and whoever is in power , the Brexit row will rumble on for years . <h> Trade relationship with EU <h> Conservatives <p> A " zero tariff , zero quota " arrangement which would mean goods travelling between the UK and Europe with no taxes , in unlimited quantities . The UK would stay outside the single market and customs union , although Northern Ireland would keep the rules of both . That would mean checks on imports and exports to ensure that British manufacturers are not breaching European standards . <h> Labour <p> Enter into a customs union with the EU which would also feature " close alignment with the single market " . The intention would be to deliver the " exact same benefits " of the status quo so that all British businesses can continue to trade with Europe on identical terms as now and there is no change to arrangements on the Irish border . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Continue trading with the EU on the same terms as now . Take a leading role within the EU to deepen economic ties between member states . If Brexit does happen , the party will push for the closest possible economic relationship including membership of the customs union and single market . <h> Green Party <p> The Greens support greater European integration and radical reform of EU institutions , such as moving legislative power to the European Parliament and abolishing the EU seat in Strasbourg . They propose a Europe-wide minimum wage , an EU carbon tariff and " fiscal transfers " within the eurozone so that richer countries subsidise the budgets of poorer ones . <h> Brexit Party <p> A " Canada-style " trade deal with no tariffs on goods between Britain and Europe , but no commitment for the two sides to align their customs or regulatory regimes . This could mean checks on all goods going between the UK and EU , including those crossing the Irish border . <h> Ukip <p> Strike a loose trade arrangement with the EU , where both sides agree not to impose tariffs on each other but otherwise keep " regulatory independence " . This would create obstacles on the trade of goods , compared to the status quo . If the EU refuses , trade on WTO terms indefinitely . <h> SNP <p> If stopping Brexit proves impossible , the party will fight to protect Scotland 's place in the single market and customs union -- before ultimately seeking to rejoin the EU as an independent country . Its manifesto says its MPs will also work to prevent Scotland 's interests being used as " bargaining chips " in future negotiations with the EU or in any future trade agreement . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> If unsuccessful in keeping the UK within the EU , Plaid will push for Britain to stay in the single market and customs union -- arguing they " are both essential for our home-grown employers and for attracting inward investment and job creation " . The party acknowledges this would be worse than EU membership because the UK would not have a say in setting the rules . <h> Summary : <p> The three pro-Leave parties all want some form of loose free-trade arrangement , although the Tories caveat that by creating a special status for Northern Ireland . If the pro-Remain parties fail to reverse Brexit they will all push for the closest trade relationship possible . Labour will offer a choice between soft Brexit and Remain . <h> Trade with rest of world <h> Conservatives <p> The Conservative manifesto pledges to strike free-trade agreements with the USA , Australia , New Zealand and Canada within three years . They also want to get trade deals with China and India in the longer term as well as other fast-growing countries in poorer parts of the world . The party says food standards and the NHS will not be up for negotiation in any trade talks . <h> Labour <p> Labour wants the new UK-EU customs union to be different from the existing customs union , so that Britain would have an independent say in any future trade deals between Europe and the rest of the world . The party would seek to block a trade agreement with the US if it included access to the UK 's health market for American firms . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Support the expansion of international trade in the face of opposition from nationalist leaders in other countries . Work with international agencies to ensure that global trade deals do not " worsen inequalities or undermine human rights " , and use the trading system to reduce corruption in poor countries . <h> Green Party <p> All trade deals must be environmentally friendly and protect employment rights . Carry out trade negotiations in public , with all documents published along with detailed assessments of their impact . Abolish " investor-state dispute settlement mechanisms " which allow companies to sue the government if they feel they are being unfairly excluded from markets . <h> Brexit Party <p> Strike free-trade agreements with as many countries as possible in order to make the most of the economic opportunities presented by Brexit . <h> Ukip <p> Halve all existing tariffs unilaterally and immediately . Set up a Commonwealth Free Trade Agreement to give preferential terms to other members of the Commonwealth . Strike trade deals with other countries , as long as they do not harm any British industry . Abolish investor-state dispute settlement mechanisms which Ukip calls " corporate courts " . <h> SNP <p> The party says a future trade deal with the United States could risk opening up the NHS to American multinational firms , as well as seeing the arrival of chlorinated chicken and hormone injected beef . Its manifesto also says its MPs will oppose any trade talks with Donald Trump until the US drops its new tariffs on Scotch whisky , introduced in October . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Do not prioritise a trade deal with the US . Ensure that any new trade agreements protect Welsh agriculture rather than immediately slashing tariffs . Give the Welsh assembly , as well as other devolved institutions , a formal say over whether or not to ratify future trade deals . <h> Summary : <p> In theory every party is in favour of expanding trade deals with other countries , but only the Conservatives hold the idea up as a top priority . The anti-Brexit parties would push to give Britain as much influence as possible over the EU 's trade policy , particularly in the event of fresh US-Europe trade talks . <h> Following EU standards <h> Conservatives <p> The political declaration attached to the Withdrawal Agreement guarantees a " level playing field " which means that UK standards could not fall below EU ones , but this is not legally binding . The Conservatives have promised to give Parliament a say on whether or not to approve any future move to reduce workers ' rights below those in Europe . They would relax rules on using state aid to invest in industry . <h> Labour <p> Dynamic alignment on rights for workers and consumers , as well as environmental protections , meaning that every time Brussels changes the law in any of these areas the UK would automatically do the same . Legally binding protection for level playing field provisions which would block any change to regulatory standards . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> The Liberal Democrats would oppose any trade deals which involved Britain lowering its regulatory standards on the ground that this would make it harder to do business with Europe . If they succeeded in keeping the UK in the EU they would urge other member states not to compromise existing standards on the environment and animal rights in any future trade deals . <h> Green Party <p> The Greens would keep existing EU regulations and work with other countries to expand them by banning factory farming , outlawing hunting for sport , ending the export of live animals and changing the Common Agricultural Policy and Common Fisheries Policy . <h> Brexit Party <p> The Brexit Party would abandon all European standards and make no commitment to a level playing field . This would allow the UK government to use public money to rescue troubled industries including the railways and steel manufacturers . There would be no future link between the EU 's regulatory standards and those which apply in Britain . <h> Ukip <p> Ukip promises to " reduce regulation to an appropriate level " by abolishing the laws businesses must follow due to our membership of the EU . But it would maintain existing laws on workers ' rights . <h> SNP <p> Pending Scottish independence , its MPs will press for the devolution of employment law so Holyrood can protect workers ' rights which it fears will be diluted after Brexit . The party 's MPs will also campaign for the UK to remain aligned with EU environmental regulations even if Brexit takes place , including sticking to future emissions standards . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Plaid has promised to threaten any moves which might " weaken the standards and rules on food safety and medicines " . If Brexit does take place the party favours keeping all existing European rules and regulations indefinitely . <h> Summary : <p> Apart from the Brexit Party and Ukip , all the parties want to keep or even increase the current level of regulation in areas such as the environment and workers ' rights . But leaving the EU would open the door to changing this in future , whatever manifesto promises are made . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Promised an extra ? 10.5bn for schools in England by 2024-25 compared to 2019-20 . Starting salaries for teachers will rise to ? 30,000 . Ofsted will be replaced with a new HM Inspector of Schools , and league tables reformed to include information about pupils ' and teachers ' wellbeing . Schools will be required to have " inclusive " and gender-neutral uniform policies . <h> Green Party <p> Promised to increase funding on schools by at least ? 4 billion per year . It would replace Ofsted with a " collaborative system of assessing and supporting schools locally " . Private schools would lose their charitable status and VAT would be levied on fees . A ' English Climate Emergency Education Act ' would be introduced to give pupils more teaching on climate change . <h> Brexit Party <p> The Brexit Party 's " contract with the people " does not include much detail on its education policies . But on schools , the party says it will " further expand parental choice " , with the document claiming that " academies and free schools have improved results " . However , the evidence for this is mixed , with performance varying between different types of academies and free schools . <h> Ukip <p> UKIP 's manifesto promises to increase school funding by ? 4 billion per year . The party would " encourage the establishment of new grammar schools " , and scrap the 50 per cent cap on faith-based selection in faith academies and free schools . It claims children are being " indoctrinated by ' teacher activists ' who promote gender confusion , climate alarmism and a hatred of our own culture and heritage " . <h> SNP <p> Education is devolved to Scotland , with SNP leader Nicola Sturgeon describing closing the gap between rich and poor pupils as her " number one priority " in government . Minister have committed ? 750m over the current Parliament to this issue but progress has been slow . International research published this week showed while pupil performance in reading is improving , it has declined in maths and science to a record low . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Plaid Cymru has said it will provide an extra ? 300m for schools and colleges in Wales . The party has said it will develop new Welsh medium schools where there is local demand . It has promised to improve teacher retention by " cutting bureaucracy " and introducing mandatory continuous professional development . A ' National Cooperative Agency for Supply Teachers ' would extend training entitlements to supply teachers . <h> Summary : <p> After the austerity years , more money is coming to schools whoever wins power . In England , Ofsted is a dividing line -- the Tories argue it raises standards and is well recognised by parents . Other parties blame it for driving away teachers . <h> Universities <h> Conservatives <p> The Conservative manifesto is tight lipped on the future of university funding . It only says the party will consider " carefully " the Augar Review , which recommended cutting tuition fees from ? 9,250 to ? 7,500 per year . It promises to " look at " interest rates on loan repayments . The party says it will tackle degree grade inflation and " strengthen academic freedom and free speech " . <h> Labour <p> Promised to abolish tuition fees and bring back maintenance grants for students . The two policies are costed in its manifesto at ? 7.2bn a year . The party has said it will introduce post-qualification admissions to higher education in England , with students applying after they have their A levels , rather than the current practice of applying on the basis of predicted grades . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Given the political damage sustained by the Lib Dems in the past over tuition fees , the party has avoided fleshing out a major policy on university funding . It repeats the wording used in previous manifestos pledging a " review of higher education finance " . However the party has promised to reinstate maintenance grants . Mental health provision in universities will be improved by legislating for a ' Student Mental Health Charter ' . <h> Green Party <p> Wants to scrap undergraduate tuition fees . It has also promised to write-off existing debt for former students who have studied under the ? 9,000 tuition fee regime . The party 's manifesto does not state how much this would cost , but acknowledges it would " add an additional sum onto the national debt " . The cost would probably run into the tens of billions . <h> Brexit Party <p> It has pledged to scrap all interest on student loans . The party has also said it will " abolish the target to push 50 per cent of young people into higher education " . The symbolic target was first set by Tony Blair in 1999 , and was finally reached for the first time in 2017-18 . <h> Ukip <p> Like the Brexit Party , UKIP have said they will " drop the artificial target " of 50 per cent of people going to university . The party says it will waive the repayment of tuition fees in subjects " vital to our national life " , listing science , technology , engineering , mathematics and medicine in this category . The waiver would be dependent on graduates working in their fields in the UK during the repayment period . <h> SNP <p> The SNP has committed to maintaining free higher education for all Scottish students who choose to study in their home nation , with " no return to tuition fees " while it remains in power . Ministers spend ? 1bn on universities every year , but the nation 's public spending watchdog warned in September that more money was needed , highlighting a 12 per cent real terms funding cut over seven years . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Promises to " address the long term brain drain of young people out of Wales " . To achieve this , it plans to provide a subsidy to students resident in Wales who study in Wales . The manifesto says those taking subjects " vital to the Welsh economy " will pay no tuition fees in Wales , mentioning healthcare , science , engineering and technology . The same applies to students from " particularly challenging backgrounds " . <h> Summary : <p> Voters have a variety of choices , with most parties offering changes to university funding or student grants to some degree . Several parties are pledging to abolish tuition fees altogether , although this comes with a significant price tag . <h> Further education and skills <h> Conservatives <p> The Tories are promising to create a new National Skills Fund worth ? 3bn over the next Parliament . Details about how it will work are vague , but the manifesto says it will provide " matching funding " for individuals and small firms to access training . The party has pledged almost ? 2bn to upgrade the college estate , and wants to launch 20 Institutes of Technology to deliver science and engineering training . <h> Labour <p> Labour has pledged to give every adult a free entitlement to six years of study for qualifications up to level six ( undergraduate degrees or equivalent vocational courses ) . The commitment would be part of a new ' National Education Service ' , to give people access to education from " cradle to grave " . The party would also bring back the Education Maintenance Allowance -- grants for 16 to 19-year-olds who stay in education . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Aims to introduce a new ' Skills Wallet ' for every adult in England . The system would involve the Government giving individuals ? 10,000 throughout their life , which could then be spent on approved education and training courses . The party has also said it will introduce a ' young people 's premium ' which would give sixth forms and FE colleges extra funding for every student from a poorer background . <h> Green Party <p> Will " revive " the FE sector by increasing the funding rate for 16 and 17-year olds , and introducing a " capital expansion fund " for sixth form providers . The party promises to increase funding for adult education across England and Wales , and would integrate this programme with its ' Green New Deal ' -- a project to decarbonise the economy . It plans to spend ? 2bn re-skilling people . <h> Brexit Party <p> Wants to " scrap " the apprenticeship levy , which it describes as " cumbersome " and blames for a collapse in apprenticeship numbers . Under the levy , larger employers have to pay a tax to fund the development of apprenticeships . The party says it will " improve tax incentives for employers to take on genuine apprentices " . <h> Ukip <p> Technical and vocational providers would be included in a UKIP push for a range of different types of schools in each area . The party has said it supports " real trade apprenticeships and apprentice degree courses " . However , it would review the apprenticeship levy , which it says " has in some cases been over-complicated and counter-productive " . <h> SNP <p> Since 2007 the SNP-run Scottish Government has invested more than ? 7bn in colleges , with over ? 600m coming in the current financial year , and says more full-time students are completing their courses . However , in May the public spending watchdog warned that the financial challenges facing colleges were intensifying , with most forecasting deficits in the next five years . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Says it will increase funding for degree apprentices in Wales . The party says it will increase the pay of college lecturers to ensure parity with school teachers in terms of base hourly pay . Public transport would be made free for all FE and sixth form students and apprentices in Wales below the age of 21 in full time education and training . <h> Summary : <p> Further education has long been a neglected part of the education system , but in this election there are encouraging signs that the parties are taking it more seriously . Reskilling adults is likely to become more important . <h> Health <p> The NHS has been a crucial topic in this election campaign ( Photo : Getty Images ) <h> NHS spending <h> Conservatives <p> Pledged to invest an extra ? 34bn cash in the NHS by 2023-24 compared to 2018-19 budgets , amounting to a 3.1 per cent increase in spending per annum . This is lower than the average 4 per cent increase per year provided up until 2010 . Will create Innovative Medicines Fund to combat cancer and autoimmune disease and introduce a national child vaccination reminder system . Will tackle gambling addiction and end hospital car parking charges for those in greatest need . <h> Labour <p> Will offer biggest spending increase of 4.3 per cent a year as part of ? 26bn " rescue package " for the NHS . It will create a public drug company to keep costs low , and introduce a " milkshake tax " on top of the existing sugary drinks levy to combat obesity . It will ban fast-food outlets near schools and crackdown on junk food advertising . Will look at minimum alcohol pricing , implement a " tobacco control plan " and offer free NHS dental check ups . Will also create a ? 7.2bn cycling and walking strategy offering free bikes to improve the populations fitness . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> The party will inject ? 7bn a year into health and social care by putting 1p on Income Tax . Further ? 10bn capital money will be invested in hospitals and equipment . Will introduce a gambling tax to treat gambling addiction and ban the use of credit cards for betting . Will restrict junk food marketing and bring in new tobacco levy and boost overall public health budgets cut from local authorities . Aims to bring in a minimum unit pricing for alcohol . <h> Green Party <p> The Green will increase funding for the NHS by at least ? 6bn per year each year until 2030 , equating to a 4.5 per cent increase on the 2018/2019 NHS budget . Says it will roll back privatisation of the health service , and build new local community health centres to focus on preventative healthcare , to ensure people live healthier lifestyles . <h> Brexit Party <p> As the party refused to publish a manifesto , its so-called " contract " to the people is far lighter in detail when it comes to health policy . That said , it insists the NHS must remain " publicly owned " . It adds a person 's postcode should not dictate the quality of care . It also rules out privatisation of the health service , and supports medical research investment to stop the taxpayer being " ripped off " by big pharma . Calls for national debate on ringfencing the NHS budget and the tax revenues that pay for it . <h> Ukip <p> Promises to be proactive in public health campaigns to prevent ill-health occurring in the first place . Demands education on nutrition and healthy lifestyles to be a compulsory part of the school curriculum . Will abolish prescription charges in England and scrap hospital car parking charges . <h> SNP <p> Health is devolved to Scotland , but the SNP is planning an NHS Protection Act at Westminster to guarantee that future trade deals will not undermine the founding principles of the health service and avoid " profit-driven exploitation " . Its MPs will also press the UK Government to match Scottish per capita NHS spending , claiming the consequent funding boost would allow Holyrood ministers to increase their own investment by more than ? 17bn by 2024/25 . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Focuses on social care investment as part of its ? 17bn health budget . Pledges to further explore how the tax system can be used to promote public health , such as a minimum price per unit of alcohol . Wants to create a National Institute for Public Health to advise on such policy without interference of " vested interests " . Suggests new planning laws to ensure greater emphasis on green spaces and cycle ways . <h> Summary : <p> Each party has pledged more funding for the NHS with Labour far outstripping its rivals . The need to utilise public health campaigns in order to save spending public money battling preventable diseases or obesity is widely recognised by all parties . But whereas most parties aim to use the tax system to fund them , the Tories do not . <h> Staffing <h> Conservatives <p> The Tories have also pledged 50,000 more nurses , although this has been disputed as it is made up of retaining 19,000 nurses . It will bring in 6,000 more GPs and 6,000 more primary care professionals , such as physiotherapists and pharmacists . Party claims this will deliver 50m extra GP appointments per year . Says it will use additional funding to bring down operating waiting times , improve A&amp;E performance and increase cancer survival rates . <h> Labour <p> The party is strangely less ambitious with its staffing pledges , promising to deliver 24,000 extras nurses and midwives . Party says it will bring in a training bursary for nurses , midwives and other health professionals . Says it will " stabilise " overstretched A&amp;E departments and expand GP training places to provide resources for 27m more appointments each year . Promises to end and reverse privatisation in the NHS . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> The Lib Dems are less ambitious than the Tories when it comes to staffing , stating it will target extra support for nursing students , inducing bursaries of specialist nurses , such as those working in mental health and learning disabilities . Promises to review future needs for all staff , and produce a " national workforce strategy " to retain more NHS workers . <h> Green Party <p> Commits to creating a " duty " for the Health Secretary to ensure there are enough health and care staff -- including nursing -- to meet the needs of the population . <h> Brexit Party <p> Pledges to abolish all " politically-imposed " hospital targets that it says distorts clinical priorities , and wants to re-open nursing and midwifery to recruitment without the need for a degree . Will also usher in 24-hour GP surgeries to relieve pressure on A&amp;E departments . <h> Ukip <p> Will prioritise training British NHS workers , rather than relying on recruiting medical staff from abroad . Party adds it will encourage the recruitment of hospital doctors and GPs by waiving repayment of tuition fees while they work in the NHS , and we will reintroduce student bursaries for nursing and midwifery students . <h> SNP <p> SNP ministers at Holyrood have promised to invest ? 250m in primary care during the current parliament and are aiming to recruit 800 extra family doctors over the next decade . But figures published this week show the GP headcount has increased by only 55 on last year , with the public spending watchdog warning that meeting the target will be very tough . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Pledges to recruit an additional 1,000 doctors , 5,000 nurses and 500 dentists for the Welsh NHS . Will free up ? 90m by cracking down on use of agency staff in the health service . <h> Summary : <p> The recruitment and retention of NHS staff is acutely understood by all parties given the pressures the health system is under . While the Conservatives have come under fire for their arithmetic on additional nurses , they are among the most ambitious in this area . <h> Mental health <h> Conservatives <p> Promises to treat mental health with the " same urgency " as physical health , and will legislate to ensure patients suffering from mental health conditions , such as anxiety and depression , have greater control over treatment . <h> Labour <p> Labour will pump an extra ? 1.6bn a year to ensure new mental health standards are " enshrined " in the NHS . A further ? 2bn will be spent modernising hospital facilities to accommodate mental health patients . It will also spend ? 845m on a new Healthy Young Minds programme to " more than double " spending on children and adolescent mental health services . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> The Lib Dems will ringfence funding from its penny increase on income tax to ensure extra investment on mental health . It will also introduce a maximum waiting time limit for mental health problems , and increase access to a broader range of " clinically effective " talking therapies . It has also pledged to give free prescriptions on the NHS to people suffering chronic mental health problems . <h> Green Party <p> Says it will focus funding on improving mental health care to put it on an equal footing to physical health . Promises " tailored and specific " provision for the particular needs of Lesbian , Gay , Bisexual , Trans , Intersex , Queer and Asexual ( LGBTIQA+ ) and the black and minority ethnic communities . <h> Brexit Party <p> The party states it wants the NHS to be a " beacon of excellent care " , but its " contract " does not mention mental health provision . <h> Ukip <h> SNP <p> A total of ? 250m has been pledged to support mental health services in Scotland over the next five years , including ? 60m for schools to improve counselling services and train staff . However , statistics published this week show that waiting time targets for young people are being missed in more than a third of cases , with more than 600 waiting for more than a year . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Pledges to increase mental health expenditure by 5 per cent every year for the next 10 years . Will also establish a 24/7 Mental Health Crisis Service for those in acute distress . <h> Social care <h> Conservatives <p> Despite claiming in August the Tories had a plan for social care ready to go , Boris Johnson has said he will build a " cross-party consensus " to develop a plan to solve the social care crisis . The party announced in the autumn an additional ? 1bn to prop up the social care system from April . It has also insisted nobody needing care should be forced to sell their home to pay for it . <h> Labour <p> Will build a " comprehensive " National Care Service for England . Will offer free personal care to all , starting with investing cash to ensure older people have immediate care needs met . Labour will also introduce a lifetime cap on personal contributions to care costs and ensure no one faces " catastrophic " care costs of more than ? 100,000 . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Perhaps the least ambitious part of the party 's health manifesto , it concentrates on rationalising the current care system involving local authorities more . It pledges to create a new care workers ' professional body to improve training and pay . It also states its wants to offer more choice at the end of life , and move towards free end-of-life social care . <h> Green Party <p> The Greens will pump an additional ? 4.5bn a year to fund councils to provide free social care to people over 65 needing support in their own homes . Says it will explore provision of free social care at home to all who need it , regardless of age . <h> Brexit Party <p> The party says it wants to introduce a new nursing qualification in social care to address the staffing crisis hitting the sector , but makes no offers beyond that . <h> Ukip <p> Will bring the social care into the NHS budget . Party insists social care should not put a person 's home and savings " in jeopardy if they have paid tax and national insurance all of their life " . Will increase social care funding in England by ? 5bn in the short term . <h> SNP <p> Personal care is already free in Scotland , with the SNP also promising to scrap fees charged for a raft of services provided by local councils in people 's own homes if it is re-elected in 2021 . However , the nation 's ageing population is steadily increasing the pressure on the system , with elderly people facing longer waits while their claims are assessed and processed . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Promises to provide free social care at the point of need , delivered by a new National Health and Social Care Service at a cost to the Welsh Government of an extra ? 300 million a year . <h> Summary : <p> Arguably the policy area that was Theresa May 's undoing in 2017 , and the scars are still felt by the Tories . The party 's manifesto ducks the issue this time around . Labour and the Greens promise an expensive free care for all . <h> Economy and Spending <p> What is each party promising to do with the economy ? ( Photo : Getty ) <h> Austerity <h> Conservatives <p> Boris Johnson promises an end to the years of austerity under David Cameron and Theresa May . Before the election the Tories were already committed to raising spending on English schools by ? 7.1bn by 2023 , on the NHS by ? 34bn by 2024 and recruiting 20,000 extra police officers . Their manifesto added new promises of ? 2.9bn including a nurse recruitment drive and a blitz on potholes . <h> Labour <p> Pledges the " largest-scale investment in modern times " , as well as another ? 10.5bn for schools , to scrap tuition fees , inject an extra ? 26bn a year into the NHS , bring in a Real Living Wage of at least ? 10 per hour for all workers . In total its manifesto envisages around ? 80bn a year more spending as Labour argues sustained investment will produce economic growth . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Committed to another ? 33bn a year of spending , with the biggest focus on providing free childcare for English two , three and four year olds by 2024 at a cost of ? 13bn . This is more than four times more than the current provision . A further ? 7bn would be allocated to health and social care . An extra ? 10.6bn more would be spent on hiring 20,000 more teachers and cutting class sizes . <h> Green Party <p> Would bring austerity to a juddering halt , spending more than ? 1tn during the five-year Parliament . It will spend ? 100bn a year to cut carbon emissions by the hugely ambitious target of 2030 . Would spend ? 6bn a year more on the NHS , ? 4.5bn on social care and fund a universal basic income at a cost of ? 89bn a year . <h> Brexit Party <p> Unsurprisingly , all of the Brexit Party 's proposals for the economy and its spending plans are predicated on the UK leaving the EU in a " clean-break " departure . A " Brexit dividend " will be raised worth ? 200bn by scrapping HS2 , " keeping " ? 13bn annual contribution to the EU , clawing back ? 7bn from the European Investment Bank and cutting the foreign aid budget by half , which it says is worth ? 40bn over a five-year term . It is disputed whether these measures would raise the money it claims . <h> Ukip <p> Says it will be able to raise ? 70bn a year by virtue of leaving the European Union , cancelling major infrastructure projects , scrapping all foreign aid and abolishing around half of all government quangos . Pledges to invest in public services , such as schools , NHS and social care . <h> SNP <p> The party 's MPs will demand an end to austerity from the Westminster government and instead press for greater investment in public services and the economy , so Scotland can feel the benefits . Its manifesto argues austerity has caused " untold damage " to communities around the UK and pledges to oppose any Government does n't start to " replace the funds lost over the last 10 years " . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Believes the UK economy is heavily skewed towards the south east of England and London . As such , it calls for an end of the " outdated " Barnet Formula that calculates the nation 's finances and demands it is replaced by an Office for Fair Funding to deliver increased funding for Wales . <h> Summary : <p> Each of the parties promise to end austerity . While the Tories ' manifesto is relatively unambitious compared with its rivals , it still promises increases in public spending . Austerity will be well and truly consigned to history should the likes of Labour or Lib Dems come close to power with spending on frontline service set to soar . <h> Capital investment <h> Conservatives <p> Pledging to oversee an " infrastructure revolution for this country " , including heavy investment in railways , ? 29bn for road-building projects and spending ? 5bn towards ensuring every address in the UK has access to full-fibre broadband . Some rail lines closed during the Beeching cuts of the 1960s would be reopened . A ? 350m Cycling Infrastructure Fund would be established . <h> Labour <p> At the heart of Labour 's plans for revitalising the economy is a ? 400bn " national transformation fund " which would invest in infrastructure , renewable energy , house insulation , railways , electric cars and low-carbon technology . It promises a massive building programme of social housing and that full-fibre broadband would be available everywhere in the UK by 2030 . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Would pump ? 130bn into the national infrastructure . Would extend and upgrade railways and stations , invest in " cutting-edge energy technologies " , including tidal and wave power . Pledge to build at least 100,000 homes for social rent each year and ensure that total annual housebuilding increases to 300,000 . <h> Green Party <p> Will fund a vast capital investment programme worth ? 95bn , including building more zero carbon homes , while " retro-fitting " existing houses with insulation and other energy-saving measures at a cost of ? 24bn . It will scrap HS2 and spend ? 2.5bn a year on cycle infrastructure . <h> Brexit Party <p> Promises to invest at least ? 50bn in local road and rail schemes in what it describes as " development-starved " areas . Says it will partner with service providers to offer free " base-level " domestic broadband in deprived areas but puts not cost to it . Will also spend ? 2.5bn to regenerate the country 's fishing and coastal communities . <h> Ukip <p> Unlike most other parties , Ukip does not have an extensive programme for capital investment , but instead pledges to scrap major infrastructure projects , such as HS2 and the expansion of Heathrow . It does promise to spend money on expanding the rail network be re-opening lines cut in the 1960s . <h> SNP <p> The amount Scotland receives in its block grant from Westminster is determined each year and partly depends on spending decisions made by the UK Government in other areas . While the Tories have pledged a ? 3.1bn " windfall " for Scotland if its wins the election , the SNP has ruled out a deal with the party -- but it could work with Labour which has promised ? 100bn . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Has called for at least an extra ? 1.5bn a year to be spent on capital investment and allocated on a " needs basis " . The money would come from the UK government raising an ? 20bn a year over the next 10 years through borrowing . <h> Summary : <p> One area of the economy that is likely to see the most significant increase in spending is capital investment . Even the Conservatives are pledging to set new fiscal rules to spend ? 100bn on infrastructure projects . Labour dwarves it with a ? 400bn plan . <h> Personal taxes and VAT <h> Conservatives <p> Committed to a " triple tax lock " , guaranteeing that they will not raise the rates of the three biggest taxes -- national insurance ( NI ) , income tax and VAT . They have indicated that they increase the NI threshold to ? 9,500 next year , with an " ultimate ambition " to lift it to ? 12,500 but no further details of the timescale . <h> Labour <p> Planned spending would be paid for by introducing a 45 per cent income tax rate on earnings over ? 80,000 and a 50 per cent rate on those with salaries of over ? 125,000 . Labour says only the top five per cent of earners would pay more under its " fairer tax " regime . National insurance rates would be frozen and Labour guarantees that VAT rates will not rise . Capital gains and dividend tax rates would be brought in line with new income tax rates . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Would raise all income rates by a penny in the pound in England , Wales and Northern Ireland , ring-fencing the ? 7bn extra cash for spending on the NHS and social care . The marriage tax allowance would be scrapped . The separate capital gains tax-free allowance would also be abolished and capital gains and salaries would instead be taxed through a single allowance . <h> Green Party <p> Plans to merge a variety of personal taxes , including employees ' national insurance , capital gains , inheritance and income tax into a single " consolidated income tax " . It says this will bring in an extra ? 20bn a year . Says it will replace the income tax threshold with Universal Basic Income , which will give ? 89 to every adult of ? 178 to families and pensioners a week . <h> Brexit Party <p> Makes no mention of income tax or National Insurance Contributions but pledges to abolish inheritance tax , which it describes as a " hated grief tax " that brings in 1 per cent of total tax revenue . <h> Ukip <p> Will raise the personal income tax allowance from ? 12,500 to ? 15,000 over the next Parliamentary term . Aims to restructure income tax into two bands of 20 per cent and 40 per cent with higher thresholds and will abolish inheritance tax ( currently ? 5.2bn per annum ) . It will also abolish stamp duty for UK citizens ' primary residences , but keep it for foreign purchases . <h> SNP <p> Scotland now sets its own rates and bands of income tax , but at Westminster the party says it will oppose tax cuts for the wealthiest and instead support a crackdown on tax avoidance and evasion . Its manifesto says its MPs will press the UK Government to freeze people 's National Insurance ( NI ) contributions and VAT rates , as well as calling for the devolution of NI to Scotland . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Would restrict income tax relief on pension contributions to the standard rate of 20 per cent , raising an estimated ? 11.5bn a year . Promises to raise employee national insurance contributions for higher and additional rate taxpayers from 2 per cent to 4 per cent pulling in around ? 2bn per annum . <h> Summary : <p> One of the areas where nearly all the parties are playing fast and loose with the truth . Most parties have pledged extra investment in public services , while suggesting tax rises will hit only the wealthiest or in the Tories ' case no one at all . But more spending must mean higher taxes or additional borrowing . <h> Business taxes <h> Conservatives <p> Government plans to cut corporation tax next year from 19 to 17 per cent would be scrapped to free up ? 6bn a year for public services . Business rates would be reduced with early cuts for pubs , music venues and small cinemas . A digital services tax would aim to ensure that major multinational companies pay " their fair share of tax " . <h> Labour <p> Corporate taxes would increase from 19 per cent to 21 per cent next April and to 26 per cent by 2023 . For small firms the rate would remain at 19 per cent until 2023 when it would become 23 per cent . A financial transactions tax would be brought in , along with a new tax on multinational firms operating in the UK but based overseas . Oil and gas firms would face a one-off windfall levy with the cash raised used to retrain workers in the industry . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Corporation Tax would be raised from 19 to 20 per cent with a pledge to " keep the rate stable with a predictable future path " . The party would triple the proposed digital services tax to six per cent . The most frequent fliers would be hit by plans to reform air passenger duty in a move that would raise around ? 5bn . A crackdown on tax avoidance is projected to raise ? 5.7bn . <h> Green Party <p> Plans to increase corporation tax from 19 per cent to 24 per cent , will raise the Bank Asset Tax . It also proposes abolishing both council tax and business rates and replacing them with a single land value tax that will also take in stamp duty on land . It believes this will capture the " real value of land , and the increased value arising from improvements to it " . <h> Brexit Party <p> Perhaps its most comprehensive policy area , the party promises to exempt 1m small businesses from corporation tax . It means all those firms with pre-tax profit of less than ? 50,000 will pay no corporation tax . <h> Ukip <p> Will keep corporation tax at 19 per cent with a view to lowering it over time . Post-Brexit it will cut VAT rates to zero on goods such as domestic fuel , sanitary products , and repairs to commercial , residential buildings . Will review council tax , and reduce business rates for high street shops , restaurants and pubs to zero with plans to replace it with an online sales tax for any online business with an annual turnover of ? 500,000 . <h> SNP <p> The party 's MPs will back an increase in the National Insurance discount businesses receive from ? 3,000 per firm per year to ? 6,000 , which it says will help relieve uncertainty caused by Brexit . As part of a crackdown on tax avoidance , it also wants to see tougher measures to improve the transparency of tax paid by international companies and a " fit for purpose " tax for online retailers . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Promises to freeze corporation tax at its current rate of 19 per cent , in a move similar to the Tories . Plaid believes this will raise ? 5bn . Taken together the tax policies will raise an extra ? 20bn , it says . <h> Summary : <p> Arguably the area of the tax regime that will be doing the heaviest lifting for most parties . Labour has suggested a vast proportion of its promises will be delivered by raising corporation tax . The Tories even abandoned their long held commitment to cut corporation tax to fund its plans . Business rates are also in line to tumble , whoever comes into power . <h> Pensions <h> Conservatives <p> The pensions triple lock , the winter fuel payment , the older person 's bus pass and other pensioner benefits would be retained , but the Tories reiterate that it is up to the BBC to fund free television licences for over-75s . Mr Johnson has said he can not promise to " magic up " money to compensate " Waspi women " hit by the change in the state pension age . <h> Labour <p> The ' triple lock ' on pension rises would be retained and Labour would guarantee the Winter Fuel Payment , free TV licences and free bus passes as universal benefits . Plans to raise the state pension age would be abandoned to leave it at 66 . Around 3.7m ' Waspi women ' , who claim they were not properly alerted to a rise in the pension age would be compensated at a total cost of ? 58bn . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Would keep the pension ' triple lock ' for the duration of the next parliament and would retain pensioner benefits such as winter fuel payments and free bus passes.The Lib Dems are committed to paying compensation to ' Waspi ' women who lost out when the state pension age went out . They say the parliamentary ombudsman would rule on the levels of compensation . <h> Green Party <p> Commits to giving all pensioners ? 178 a week -- ? 10 higher than the current highest possible pension payment . Says it will look to address the " injustice " affected by hundreds of thousands of Waspi women . <h> Brexit Party <p> Promises to launch a " review " of the position of Waspi women , which it says were " unexpectedly short-changed " by the rise in the state pension age . <h> Ukip <p> Describes the state pension as a " Ponzi scheme " . Will maintain the triple lock on the state pension and review the national insurance system to ensure it delivers higher , more sustainable pensions . Will " deliver a solution " to Waspi women . <h> SNP <p> With pensions reserved to Westminster , the party will continue to support the " triple lock " , ensuring they continue to rise by inflation , earnings or 2.5 per cent -- whatever is highest . Its MPs will also oppose any increase to the state pension age , continue to support the WASPI campaign and argue for the reversal of the cut to Pension Credit . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Will compensate the women affected by the rise in state pension age , and promises to maintain the triple lock on state pensions . <h> Summary : <p> Pensioners can breathe easy in this election as , on the whole , they are the best looked after demographic in this election . Almost all parties pledge to keep the " triple lock " . Waspi women will be worst off under the Tories , and will be completely compensated by Labour in a major ? 26bn pledge . <h> Northern Powerhouse <h> Conservatives <p> There is a commitment to building Northern Powerhouse Rail ( previously known as High Speed 3 ) between Leeds and Manchester , and then " focus on Liverpool , Tees Valley , Hull , Sheffield and Newcastle " . The Tories would also press ahead with the Midland Rail Hub scheme , improving links between Birmingham , Leicester , Nottingham , Coventry , Derby , Hereford and Worcester . <h> Labour <p> Promises a ' radical decentralisation of power in Britain ' , including relocating part of the Treasury to the North of England and building regional offices of government . The projects would boost the economy of the north , helping to create hundreds of thousands of jobs , the party says . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Promise to " kickstart a devolution revolution " with a ? 50bn regional balancing programme to spread investment across all parts of the UK . Say they would put significant resources into infrastructure projects in the Northern Powerhouse and the Midlands Engine regions and boost research and development outside the ' golden triangle ' of Oxford-Cambridge-London . <h> Green Party <p> Will scrap HS2 , which is championed by many northern leaders but commits to ushering in a new " golden era " of ril travel , opening up links between towns and cities in the north and the midlands . <h> Brexit Party <p> Makes no specific mention of the Northern Powerhouse , but Nigel Farage has come under fire from northern leaders over its promise to scrap HS2 . <h> Ukip <p> Plans to scrap HS2 but will create free ports to " turbo-charge " the north of England in areas such as Immingham and Grimsby , Hull Port , the Hull and Humber rivers , Tees and Hartlepool , Liverpool , the Tyne , and Manchester airport . <h> SNP <p> Nicola Sturgeon has previously spoken of her ambition for Scotland to become the UK 's " real Northern Powerhouse " and her party has criticised the UK economy 's reliance on London . It has also called for the HS2 rail link to be extended to Scotland , something that is promised by Labour in its manifesto , which could also be a bargaining point between the two parties . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Wants to scrap the " wasteful and environmentally damaging " HS2 project , and plough the money saved into transport infrastructure more " fairly " across the UK . <h> Summary : <p> Most parties pledge to devolve decision-making to the regions , particularly the north . For northern leaders , pushing on with HS2 is paramount to deliver the idea of the Northern Powerhouse . Fewer than half of the parties commit to delivering the rail project , however . The Tories do pledge to push on with HS3 or " Crossrail for the North " , while Labour commits to the entire scheme . <h> Borrowing and debt <h> Conservatives <p> Promise not borrow to fund day-to-day spending , but would " invest thoughtfully and responsibly in infrastructure " . The IFS think-tank estimates that Tory borrowing would be just over two per cent of GDP which is broadly in line with their aim of balancing the current budget . The party insists its spending plans are consistent with their commitment to controlling the UK 's debts . <h> Labour <p> Argues the UK needs to " borrow to invest in long-term productive projects that will both save our planet and stand our public sector in good stead financially for decades to come " . The IFS thinktank says this implies borrowing of around four per cent of GDP without taking the ' Waspi women ' pledge into account . Labour says it aims to balance the current budget . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Say they would take advantage of historically low interest rates to increase borrowing for investment . The IFS thinktank said the Lib Dem proposals implied lower borrowing levels than suggested by the Labour or Conservative manifestos . It said : " They would appear to be the only one of these three parties which would put debt on a decisively downward path . " <h> Green Party <p> Its plans will mean an eye-watering additional operational expenditure of ? 141.5bn a year , which it says will be paid for by a mix of tax reforms and savings measures . It will borrow ? 94.4bn for capital expenditure . It says it " appreciates these are large numbers " . <h> Brexit Party <p> Does not go into specifics about what would be its fiscal rules if in power , but its priorities suggest that additional investment will come from its Brexit dividend . <h> Ukip <p> Rules out additional borrowing and aims to balance the national budget by reducing the budget deficit to zero and thereafter paying off our national debt . <h> SNP <p> As well as the annual block grant from Westminster , SNP ministers can now borrow up to ? 450m per year up to a maximum total of ? 3bn -- but the party wants these limits to be increased . Its manifesto says having greater flexibility would allow the Scottish Government to " invest in infrastructure and grow our economy " more effectively . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Will increase borrowing for investment in capital infrastructure to the tune of around ? 200bn over 10 years . On day to day spending will raise revenue via higher taxes rather than additional borrowing . <h> Summary : <p> Most parties pledge to devolve decision-making to the regions , particularly the north . For northern leaders , pushing on with HS2 is paramount to deliver the idea of the Northern Powerhouse . Fewer than half of the parties commit to delivering the rail project , however . The Tories do pledge to push on with HS3 or " Crossrail for the North " , while Labour commits to the entire scheme . <h> Infrastructure <p> Commuters wait for trains at Clapham Junction train station in London , Monday , Jan. 8 , 2018 . Thousands of commuters face a week of mayhem from Monday as Southern , Greater Anglia and South Western Railway staff plough ahead with planned strike action . ( AP Photo/Frank Augstein ) <h> Heathrow <h> Conservatives <p> Boris Johnson has been a long-standing opponent of Heathrow expansion but as Prime Minister has softened his position . Parliament has backed in principle a third runway , but the Tories offer only luke-warm support : making clear it is a private sector project and that Heathrow must show it can meet obligations on air quality and noise and that there is a realistic business case . There will be no new public money . <h> Labour <p> No mention of Heathrow in its manifesto , but shadow chancellor John McDonnell , a staunch opponent of expansion , suggested last month that a Labour government might scrap the project on the grounds that it clashes with the party 's pledges to tackle climate change . Labour previously gave its MPs a free vote in the Commons on Heathrow , and its lack of inclusion in the manifesto leaves the door open . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> All expansion on major London airports including Heathrow , Gatwick or Stansted would be banned , as would any proposals for a new airport in the Thames Estuary . All domestic flights would have to meet new rules on emisisons , with aircraft obliged to meet a " zero carbon fuels blending requirement " . <h> Green Party <p> All airport expansion -- including at Heathrow -- would be banned across England and Wales , while a new carbon tax would be applied to aviation fuel on domestic flights . VAT exemption for domestic flights would be scrapped . All advertising for flights would be banned . People who take more than one return flight a year , including the 15 per cent of people who take 70 per cent of flights , would have to pay a Frequent Flyer Levy . <h> Brexit Party <p> No mention of Heathrow , airport expansion , flights or emissions in the party 's " contract with the people " . <h> Ukip <p> Third runway at Heathrow airport would be blocked on the grounds that it would " destroy many villages and listed buildings " and increase pollution in the local area . The party is not , however , opposed to any airport expansion : instead it would back a second runway at Gatwick airport and encourage investment in regional airports . <h> SNP <p> The party still officially supports the construction of a third runway at Heathrow , but in May Nicola Sturgeon indicated the policy may be reversed after she declared a climate emergency . The SNP manifesto points out that many of Scotland 's remote and rural communities rely on air travel , with trials of low and zero emission flights set to begin in the Highlands in 2021 . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> The party is opposed to a third runway at Heathrow on cost and environmental grounds and its MPs will vote in Parliament against any expansion . Plaid says although Heathrow claims that expansion would cost ? 14bn , the figure could be as high as ? 30bn . <h> Summary : <p> The issue of Heathrow expansion has slipped down the political agenda in recent years but is bound to come back when the airport tries to push ahead with the project . Tories and Labour have both tried to skirt the issue because of the views of senior figures with constituencies near to the airport . Unsurprisingly , the biggest opponents are the Greens and Lib Dems . <h> Railways including fares &amp; HS2 <h> Conservatives <p> Investment in Northern Powerhouse Rail and the Midlands Rail Hub . Many of the smaller Beeching lines axed in the 1960s would be restored . Contactless ticketing extended to 200 more stations in the South East . Metro mayors would be given control over local rail services . HS2 would be put on the back-burner , after the Oakervee review found costs could be as high as ? 81bn and the northern leg not delivered until 2040 . <h> Labour <p> Railways brought back under public ownership to make fares " simpler and more affordable " , reduce fragmentation and increase staffing levels . A new Crossrail for the North would be introduced and HS2 would be delivered in full up to Scotland as part of a wider network of high-speed railways . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> National rail network to be extended with smaller stations reopened . Trains converted to ultra low emissions by 2035 . Rail fares for commuters and season ticket holders frozen for a parliament . Support for HS2 , Northern Powerhouse Rail and Crossrail 2 but with greater controls on cost , accountability and potential damage to habitats and woodland . Open up franchise bidding process to public sector companies , local authorities and not-for-profit organisations . <h> Green Party <p> Extend rail network to remove bottlenecks , improve journey times and increase freight capacity and reopen closed stations . HS2 cancelled completely to fund rail improvements . All railway lines between cities electrified . Short-distance rail franchises handed to councils or groups of councils to give local people more power . All railways brought back into public ownership within 10 years . <h> Brexit Party <p> Scrap HS2 and use money to invest at least ? 50bn in local road and rail schemes in the regions who have been cut off from or not benefited from the growth of the capital . <h> Ukip <p> HS2 would be scrapped altogether on cost and environmental grounds . Door left open to part-public ownership of railways , including a new government-owned company to run failing franchises . <h> SNP <p> The party wants the work of Network Rail to be devolved to Scotland , so ministers can have greater control over how the system operates , and has argued for HS2 to be extended north of the border . Regulated fares are set to rise by 3.2 per cent in January in line with England and Wales , but off-peak fares will be held at 2.2 per cent . Ministers say any fare freeze would hit the public purse . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> HS2 project would be scrapped altogether as it is " wasteful and environmentally harmful " . There would be a trans-Wales railway to connect Wales ' coastal communities . <h> Summary : <p> There is little support for HS2 across the political parties , with only Labour and the Lib Dems fully in favour . A common theme throughout the pledges is for passengers and local communities to be given better access and control over rail services -- a clear reaction to recent problems of long-running delays and cancellations by the major train companies . <h> Housing <h> Conservatives <p> At least one millions new homes over the next Parliament . Rough sleeping abolished by the end of the next parliament , paid for by new stamp duty surcharge on non-UK resident buyers . <h> Labour <p> Department for Housing created , new ' use it or lose it ' taxes on developers on stalled housing developments , zero carbon standard for new homes , and 150,000 new social homes a year . Private rents capped in line with inflation , no fault evictions scrapped . Give local communities a greater say over new local developments . <h> Summary : <p> There has been a shift towards support for more social homes across the political parties , and greater support for renters -- with most parties pledging to axe no fault evictions . There 's also a big emphasis on energy efficiency for all new-builds . For all the pledges of hundreds of thousands of new homes a year , there is still a challenge over where they will be built . <h> Flood defences <h> Conservatives <p> The government has faced criticism over its response to flooding in the past year , so the Conservatives have stepped up their pledge on flood defences , promising ? 4bn in new funding to protect communities from flooding . <h> Labour <p> Extra ? 5.6bn in funding to improve flood defences , with areas at risk in north west England , Yorkshire and the East Midlands given priority . Fire services would be given power to coordinate emergency response to local floods , while planning guidance for new developments in flood risk areas would be reviewed by a Labour government . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Investment in restoration of peatlands , heathland , native woodlands and wetlands to protect against floods as well as absorb carbon . Greater emphasis on flood defences in planning guidelines . <h> Summary : <p> Recent major flooding in 2019 in Derbyshire , Yorkshire and the Midlands has pushed the issue higher up the political agenda . Most of the parties are concentrating on natural environment responses to mitigate against the worst deluges , such as rewilding of land and large scale tree-planting . <h> Road-building <h> Conservatives <p> Road-building and improvements on major highways and local roads to be paid for out of ? 28.8bn investment fund , as part of a wider National Infrastructure Strategy . Upgrading the A55 in north Wales and deliver the M4 relief road to improve links with England . <h> Labour <p> Less focus on roads than other forms of transport , but adoption of a Vision Zero approach to UK road safety , which aims to stop all deaths and serious injuries .
