The party 's manifesto rails against " excessive " signage and road furniture , speed cameras and speed bumps . <h> SNP <p> A major ? 3bn project to dual the A9 between Perth and Inverness started in 2015 and is due to finish in 2025 , with a similar scheme on the A96 from Inverness to Aberdeen due to end in 2030 . After a series of delays the Aberdeen Western Peripheral Route also opened in February after four years of building work , significantly reducing journey times for local residents . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Very little reference to road-building , with a greater emphasis on public transport and environmentally friendly ways of travel . The party would introduce a bicycle use reward scheme to encourage people to stop using cars and reduce congestion . <h> Summary : <p> Road-building is an area where the parties are at their most diverse in policy pledges -- with clear support for public transport over car use from the Lib Dems , Greens and Plaid Cymru . <h> Electric cars <h> Conservatives <p> The Conservatives are planning to invest ? 1bn in a fast-charging network for electric cars and vehicles , and will consult " on the earliest date " the sale of new conventional petrol and diesel cars can be phased out . An additional ? 220m has been earmarked to help develop the UK 's first all-electric bus town , the location of which is still being decided , and new low-fare high-frequency ' Superbus ' networks . <h> Labour <p> Labour hopes to position the UK at the forefront of the development and manufacture of ultra-low emission vehicles , and has set its sights on ending the sales of new combustion engine-powered vehicles by 2030 . Charging infrastructure and electric community car clubs will also be allocated cash , and the transition of public-sector car fleets and public buses to zero-emissions vehicles will also be fast-tracked . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Under the Lib Dems , every new car and small van sold by 2030 will be electric . Jo Swinson 's party hopes to accelerate the adoption of electric vehicles ( EVs ) by overhauling how they 're taxed , with plans to slash VAT on EVs to 5 per cent . The rate of installing car charging points , including residential on-street chargers as well as ultra-fast service stops , will be increased . <h> Green Party <p> While even electric vehicles produce pollution , low-emission vehicles represent an improvement on the current situation , according to the Greens . The party will incentivise the replacement of diesel and petrol vans , lorries and coaches with electricity-powered equivalents , and will require all existing petrol and motorway service stations to offer charging points by 2025 . Sales of new petrol and diesel-fuelled vehicles will be halted by 2030 . <h> Brexit Party <p> No mention is made of electric cars in the Brexit Party 's " contract with the people " . <h> Ukip <p> While vowing its support for open , free-market competition between petrol , diesel and electric vehicles , a Ukip government would end subsidies and vehicle tax exemptions for electric cars . Off-street parking and charging point provision in new housing and industrial developments would be encouraged through the local planning process , and the party claims it would support free-market solutions to increase charging station installation across England . <h> SNP <p> The SNP-led Scottish Government has committed to phase out new petrol and diesel cars and vans by 2032 , eight years ahead of the UK , and wants Westminster to follow suit . More immediately , in September ministers announced a ? 17m fund to help Scots buy less polluting ultra-low emission vehicles ( ULEVs ) by taking advantage of attractive loans . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Eight of the counties with the lowest number of public electric car charging points per person across Britain are found in Wales , leaving the country in danger of being left behind in the oncoming electric car revolution , Plaid Cymru has cautioned . The party has pledged its support to make the switch to an electric transport system by 2030 , and intends to work towards a wholly electric fleet of public sector vehicles . <h> Summary : <p> Lowering the current government 's target for ending the sale of new petrol and diesel cars and vehicles from 2040 to 2030 is a common goal shared by many of the parties , and the majority back the installation of more charging points across the UK in a bid to prepare for the impending electrical car revolution . The endorsement of electric car fleets for community use is another recurring theme . <h> Broadband <h> Conservatives <p> Boris Johnson 's party has pledged to bring full-fibre and gigabit-capable broadband to every home and business across the UK by 2025 , alongside ? 5bn in public funding to connect premises which are not commercially viable in the hardest-to-reach 20 per cent of England . This will double the party 's previous commitment to supporting roll-out to the hardest 10 per cent , it announced in October . <h> Labour <p> One of Labour 's most highly-publicised electoral promises has been free full-fibre broadband for every home in the country by 2030 . Under the name British Broadband , the scheme would involve bringing Openreach ( BT 's home connectivity division ) under public ownership . Its operating costs will be covered by the taxation of multinationals , including tech giants , and jobs for all existing broadband infrastructure and retail workers will be guaranteed . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> All new homes built from 2022 under a Liberal Democrat government will have access to ultra-fast broadband , while ensuring all existing households and businesses are able to connect to super-fast broadband . Small and medium-sized businesses will be prioritised in the roll-out of hyper-fast broadband , and special focus will be given to connecting rural areas which are likely to have poor overall connectivity . <h> Green Party <p> A commitment to rolling out high-speed broadband and better connecting rural communities through reliable broadband and mobile internet , " delivered through councils who understand local connection needs " are the Green Party 's two connectivity policies outlined in their manifesto . <h> Brexit Party <p> Nigel Farage 's Brexit Party pledges to partner with service providers to bring " free base level domestic broadband " to deprived regions , and to introduce free Wi-Fi access to all public transport . <h> Ukip <p> Instead of backing the installation of fibre broadband in every home , Ukip wants to build a network of well-connected business incubators , known as net centres , in digitally deprived areas . These will allow start-ups and small-to-medium businesses to take advantage of ultra-high-speed connectivity it says will be measured in gigabits rather than the slower megabits . <h> SNP <p> The Scottish Government is investing ? 600m with the aim of delivering superfast broadband to all of the nation 's homes and offices by the end of the current Parliament in 2021 . The programme has been hit by contractual delays and it now seems unlikely the target will be met , but ministers say it is still far more ambitious than any other plan across the UK . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Creating a publicly-owned Welsh broadband infrastructure and guaranteeing access to full-fibre broadband to every home and business in Wales by 2025 are among Plaid Cymru 's proposed communications infrastructure projects . The Welsh government announced ? 10m in funding for projects concentrating on delivering super-fast broadband to poorly served communities in mostly rural areas of the country during a debate on digital connectivity last month . <h> Summary : <p> Providing households in areas with low levels of internet connectivity with improved access is a priority across all parties with the exception of Ukip , which advocates for giving businesses the means to access faster connections instead . Labour , the Lib Dems and the Brexit party have voiced their commitment to delivering home broadband for free , though the details on how such a project would be funded differ . <h> Environment <p> Where do the parties stand on protecting the environment ? ( Photo : Getty Images ) <h> Climate change and net zero <h> Conservatives <p> Pledges to lead the global fight against climate change after the government became , in June , the first major economy to promise to become carbon neutral , by 2050 -- a pledge that was welcomed although many said it should be done sooner . Will use the UK 's position hosting the UN Climate Change Summit in Glasgow in 2020 to put pressure on other nations to match its ambition . But believes that the North Sea oil and gas industry has a long future ahead and plans to support the industry in the next Parliament . <h> Labour <p> Committed to put the UK on track to be carbon neutral within the 2030s -- after initially considering a concrete target of 2030 -- and go faster if credible pathways can be found . This is still more ambitious than the Conservative party target . Create a National Investment Bank to provide ? 250 billion of loans for enterprise , infrastructure and innovation over 10 years to finance the transition to a low-carbon economy . Promises to create at least one million unionised jobs as part of what it 's calling its Green New Deal . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Promises to deliver a ten-year emergency programme to cut greenhouse gas emissions substantially straightaway and to be entirely carbon neutral by 2045 at the latest -- five years ahead of the Conservative pledge but 10 years behind Labour . Wants the UK to take a leading global role in tackling the climate emergency . Will insulate all 2.5 million of the country 's low-income homes by 2025 , supported by a new ? 6bn fund over five years . <h> Green Party <p> The party has the most ambitious target of making the UK carbon neutral -- pledging to do so by 2030 . As you might expect the party has the most ambitious set of environmental policies . They do n't come cheap at an estimated cost of ? 100bn a year , a figure which has raised a few eyebrows and questions about where the money will come from -- but which the party says would be money well spent -- transforming the economy and its prospects . <h> Brexit Party <p> As a new party with a much narrower focus than most of its rivals , it is maybe not much of a surprise that the Brexit Party 's " contract " says less about climate change and the environment than any other party -- although it does promise to announce an unspecified " global initiative " at the UN at some point . Whereas UKIP is openly dismissive of moves to tackle climate change , the Brexit party opts to skirt the issue altogether -- not mentioning the term at all . <h> SNP <p> Scotland currently has the world 's toughest legally-binding emissions reductions targets , with SNP ministers committing to reach net zero emissions by 2045 , five years ahead of the UK target . The party 's manifesto says its MPs will press UK ministers to match the Scottish targets but also warns that if Westminster 's timetable slips , there will be a knock-on effect north of the border . <h> Biodiversity <h> Conservatives <p> Promises to invest in nature , with a ? 640 million new Nature for Climate fund to support natural systems to soak up emissions . This will build on the party 's support for creating a new forest -- the Great Northumberland Forest in the north of England . In total , the party pledges to grow an additional 75,000 acres of trees a year- or about 30 million trees -- by the end of the next Parliament , as well as restoring peatland . <h> Labour <p> Pledged to plant two billion new trees by 2040 -- or 100 million a year -- the most of any party . Will introduce a Climate and Environment Emergency Bill setting out in law robust , binding new standards for decarbonisation , nature recovery , environmental quality and habitats and species protection . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Will plant 60 million trees a year and introduce requirements for the greater use of sustainably harvested wood in construction . Will set legally binding targets for improving water , air , soil and biodiversity , supported by at least ? 18 billion over five years . Plans to establish a Department for Climate Change and Natural Resources . <h> Green Party <p> Promises to plant 700 million new trees and to make half of all farms grow trees by 2030 . To reduce pesticide and fungicide use by at least half by weight by 2022 , phase out all non-agricultural uses of pesticides , and immediately ban the most harmful substances . Maintain a moratorium on production and import of genetically modified ( GM ) foods , including food from animals fed on GM feed . <h> Brexit Party <p> It promises to plant an unspecified number of " millions " of trees . <h> SNP <p> Earlier this week the SNP pledged to plant 36m trees in Scotland by 2030 to slow climate change , support biodiversity and increase rural employment across the country . Its manifesto says it will also press UK ministers to create new woodland , working towards an overall target of 60m trees being planted every year in the UK by 2025 . <h> Energy <h> Conservatives <p> The UK 's offshore wind industry is already the biggest in the world and the party promises to more than quadruple its current capacity to 40GW by 2030 -- by which point it will be providing about a third of the UK 's electricity . Advocates of renewable energy would also like to see it relaxing an effective ban on onshore windfarms by reintroducing subsidies , although it 's not made any commitment to do so . Having placed a moratorium on fracking in England ( it does n't happen elsewhere in the UK ) and has officially ruled out relaxing the ban . However , it appeared to leave the door open for change arguing that it would not support fracking " unless the science shows categorically that it can be done safely " . <h> Labour <p> Will introduce a windfall tax on oil companies , so that the companies which knowingly damaged the climate will help cover the costs . Pledges to deliver nearly 90 per cent of electricity and 50 per cent of heat from renewable and low-carbon sources by 2030 . Will build 7,000 new offshore wind turbines , 2,000 new onshore wind turbines , enough solar panels to cover 22,000 football pitches . Will permanently ban fracking and build new nuclear power where needed for energy security . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Pledges to end fossil fuel subsidies by 2025 , and provide ' Just Transition ' funding for areas and communities negatively affected by the transition to net zero greenhouse gas emissions . Accelerate the deployment of renewable power and build more connections to continental power supplies to guarantee security of supply . Most ambitiously , it aims to be producing at least 80 per cent of the country 's electricity supply from renewable sources by 2030 , about double what it is now -- a target that won it praise among campaigners . <h> Green Party <p> Will remove subsidies to the oil and gas industries and apply a carbon tax on all fossil fuel imports and domestic extraction . Introduce support and incentives to accelerate wind energy development , with a target for wind to provide around 70 per cent of the UK 's electricity by 2030 . Ban fracking , and other unconventional forms of fossil fuel extraction . Phase out of the UK 's remaining coal plants and coal mines , ensuing a just transition for workers affected . Prohibit the construction of nuclear power stations . <h> Brexit Party <p> Post Brexit , the party promises to cut VAT rates to zero on domestic fuel -- saving an average ? 65 per household . <h> SNP <p> At Westminster , SNP MPs will propose a Green Energy Deal with the aim of ensuring that renewable energy schemes get the long-term certainty needed to support investment . The party is also proposing a Net Zero Fund that would set aside an expected ? 8.5bn of tax revenues from North Sea oil and gas and channel it into green projects . SNP ministers have also set out a policy of " no support " for fracking in Scotland , although they stopped short of an outright legal ban . <h> Air Pollution <h> Conservatives <p> Will support clean transport to ensure clean air , as well as setting strict new laws on air quality . Promises to consult on the earliest date by which it can phase out the sale of new petrol and diesel vehicles -- which is currently set at 2040 . Said its first budget will prioritise electric vehicle infrastructure including a national plug-in network and gigafactory . <h> Labour <p> Pledged to tackle air pollution in part through a transport programme focused on creating better , publicly accessible local transport systems . By improving public transport , it aims to help people to become less reliant on their cars , and to improve quality of life in our towns and cities . To this end , it will increase funding available for cycling and walking -- although it does n't say by how much . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Promises that , by 2030 , every new car and small van sold is electric . Invest in public transport , buses , trams and railways to enable people to travel more easily while reducing their impact on the environment . Accelerate the transition to ultra-low-emission transport -- cars , buses and trains -- through taxation , subsidy and regulation . Dedicate 10 percent of the transport budget to walking and cycling . Introduce London-stye Ultra-Low Emission Zones to ten other towns and cities in England and ensure that all private hire vehicles and new buses licensed to operate in urban areas are ultra-low-emission or zero-emission vehicles by 2025 -- providing ? 2 billion to support this transformation . <h> Green Party <p> End the sale of new petrol and diesel fuelled vehicles by 2030 . Create a network of electric vehicle charging points across the country . Require all existing petrol stations and motorway service stations to offer electric vehicle charging points by 2025 . Stop the building of new runways and all increased road capacity -- a move it says will save thousands of acres of countryside every year and protect people from the harm of increased air pollution . <h> Brexit Party <p> There is no mention of air pollution in the Brexit Party 's ' Contract with the People ' . <h> SNP <p> The Transport Bill passed in October gives councils the powers to introduce low-emission zones , which levy daily fees on polluting vehicles entering certain parts of cities . Glasgow will be the first to introduce one by the end of 2022 , with similar plans in Edinburgh , Dundee and Aberdeen . Green groups have criticised the proposal as being too weak and too slow . <h> Greenhouse gas emissions <h> Conservatives <p> The party has pledged ? 800m to develop new technology to capture CO2 before it gets into the atmosphere , known as carbon capture and storage ( CCS ) -- and ? 500m to help carbon-intensive industries reduce their footprints . But no policy to tackle aviation emissions , a major source of greenhouse gases . Will look to cut emissions -- and reduce energy bills -- by investing ? 9.2 billion in the energy efficiency of homes , schools and hospitals . <h> Labour <p> Labour tabled the motion which led to the UK Parliament declaring a climate and environmental emergency , which it did earlier this year , becoming the first parliament in the world to do so . While the Conservatives have committed to ending sales of new petrol and diesel vehicles by 2040 , Labour will aim for 2030 . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Would accelerate the rapid take-up of electric vehicles ( EVs ) by reforming vehicle taxation , cutting VAT on EVs to 5 per cent and speeding up the installation of charging points , including residential on-street points and ultra-fast chargers at service stations . Place a moratorium on the development of new runways in the UK , opposing any expansion of Heathrow , Gatwick or Stansted and any new airport in the Thames Estuary . Increase tax on international flights to focus on those who fly the most , while reducing costs for those who take one or two international return fights per year . Would ban fracking . <h> Green Party <p> Promise to spend ? 2.5 billion a year on new cycleways and footpaths , built using sustainable materials , such as woodchips and sawdust . Create a new ' golden age ' of train by opening new rail connections that remove bottlenecks , increase rail freight capacity , speed up journeys and increase the frequency of trains.Prepare for the rapid decommissioning of North Sea oil rigs and the phasing out of the UK 's remaining coal plants and coal . <h> Brexit Party <p> The party has said it will scrap controversial HS2 high-speed rail link -- a move that could reduce greenhouse gas emissions as the path threatens areas of woodland . <h> SNP <p> As well as its net zero by 2045 pledge , the SNP ministers have pledged to phase out new petrol and diesel cars and vans in Scotland by 2032 , eight years of the UK Government 's target . The party says this will be delivered by electrifying the road network and doubling investment in " active travel " -- such as improving walking and cycling routes -- to ? 80m per year . <h> Waste/recycling <h> Conservatives <p> After China stopped receiving large quantities of the UK 's waste , the spotlight has been put on the issue of where our waste goes -- with much being sent to developing countries that are ill-equipped to deal with it . The party would ban waste exports to all non-OECD countries and will only send it to nations with adequate facilities to recycle them . Penalties for fly-tipping will be increased and those on community sentences will be made to clean up parks and streets . <h> Labour <p> Will work with local authorities to reduce food waste and " learn from the Labour government in Wales " , where recycling rates have increased sharply in recent years . It will also set up a National Food Commission to tackle hunger and cut down on waste . The party points out that a quarter of all food purchased is wasted every year , equivalent to over 20 million tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions , costing over ? 20 billion . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Introduce a legally binding recycling target of 70 per cent -- compared to around 50 per cent now . Extend household food waste collection schemes to at least 90 per cent of homes by 2024 -- also compared to about 50 per cent now . Introduce a National Food Strategy , including the use of public procurement policy , to promote the production and consumption of healthy , sustainable and affordable food and cut down on food waste . <h> Green Party <p> Require manufacturers and retailers to pay the full cost of recycling and disposing of the packaging they produce -- something that the existing government is looking at on a smaller scale . Argues that a ' circular economy ' will underpin its proposed green industrial revolution , ' designing out ' waste and pollution and keeping products and materials in use . Recycling and repairing will be made easier , reducing the need to buy new , expensive products on a regular basis , it says . <h> Brexit Party <p> The part wants the UK to recycle its own waste and make it illegal for it to be exported across the world to be burnt , buried or dumped at sea . <h> SNP <p> Under plans announced in May , Scotland is set to become the first part of the UK to introduce a Deposit Return Scheme for drinks containers in an effort to boost recycling rates . Plastic and glass bottles or aluminium drinks cans sold in shops , pubs and restaurants will carry an extra 20p surcharge , which can be reclaimed by customers when they are returned empty . <h> Oceans/plastic <h> Conservatives <p> Will establish a new ? 500 million Blue Planet Fund to help protect oceans from plastic pollution , warming sea temperatures and overfishing.Will " continue to lead diplomatic efforts " to protect 30 per cent of the world 's oceans by 2030 . Introduce a levy to increase the proportion of recyclable plastics in packaging and a deposit return scheme for plastic and glass . Pledged ? 4 billion for new flood defences as rising sea levels threaten ever greater floods . <h> Labour <p> Will tackle the plastic pollution problem by making " producers responsible for the waste they create and for the full cost of recycling or disposal , encouraging more sustainable design and manufacturing . " It also pledges end the export of plastic waste to reduce our contribution to ocean pollution , but did n't put a timeline on this . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Ban non-recyclable single use plastic within three years . Establish a ? 5 billion fund for flood prevention and climate adaptation over the course of the parliament to improve flood defences , and introduce high standards for flood resilience for buildings and infrastructure in flood risk areas . Set up a ' blue belt ' of marine protected areas covering at least 50 per cent of UK waters by 2030 , in partnership with UK overseas territories . There is no policy to address North Sea oil and gas . <h> Green Party <p> Ban the production of single-use plastics for use in packaging and invest in research and development into alternatives to plastic . <h> Brexit Party <p> Pledges to invest ? 2.5 billion in fishing and coastal communities , adding that Brexit would allow the UK to recover control of a 200 mile exclusive economic zone which would create the opportunity to regenerate coastal communities . <h> SNP <p> As well as the Deposit Return Scheme , which it is hoped will be up and running within two years , Scotland also banned the sale and manufacture of plastic-stemmed cotton buds in October . SNP ministers are also consulting on a proposal to create Europe 's largest marine protected area off the Western Isles , with the aim of protecting coral reefs and other marine life from interference . <h> Work &amp; Benefits <p> A Universal Credit sign in the window of the Job Centre in Westminster ( Photo by Jack Taylor/Getty Images ) <h> Disability <h> Conservatives <p> The party will publish a new National Strategy for Disabled People before the end of next year . This will combine existing commitments to improve the benefits system with proposals to increase access to housing , education , jobs and transport . There is a pledge to reduce the disability employment gap . <p> Labour <p> Alongside changes to benefits , a new Department for Women and Equalities will oversee changes including a requirement that employers are better trained to accommodate disabled workers and a mandatory reporting on any disability pay-gap for companies with more than 250 employees . Disability leave will be paid and recorded separately from sick leave . <p> Liberal Democrats <p> An extra ? 6bn per annum will be invested in the social security system , including a pilot scheme rewarding employers for investing in their employees ' mental wellbeing . Cuts to the Employment Support Allowance will be reversed . More stations will be made accessible for wheelchairs . <p> Green Party <p> Alongside its plans to overhaul benefits , the party will introduce measures including a requirement for councils to draw up disability housing plans and increase the number of homes built to disabled mobility standards . There will be increased support for disabled people to enter politics and stand for office . <p> Brexit Party <p> The party 's proposed " contract " with the British people makes no specific mention of policy for the disabled . It proposes changes to the Universal Credit benefit ( see below ) . <p> UKIP <p> The party states that it is committed to protecting the rights of the disabled and supports their " inclusion in the workplace whenever that is possible " . It proposes an increase in public toilet provision with more disabled access . <h> SNP <p> A raft of disability benefits are in the process of being devolved to Scotland , including Personal Independence Payments and Disability Living Allowance , which are being rolled out in phases . The party 's manifesto says its MPs at Westminster have been " instrumental " in forcing UK ministers to rethink proposed cuts to disability benefits and promises to keep up the pressure . <p> Plaid Cymru <p> The party proposes a return to sheltered employment schemes for those with disabilities , which will serve as a " stepping stone " towards full employment . It also proposes an Autism Act for Wales , giving full protection under equalities law to those with the condition . Disabled people should not face the same benefits threats and sanctions that the able-bodied do in seeking employment . <p> Summary : <p> The parties pledges attempt to address problems with the benefits system and action to ensure the disabled have fair access to the jobs market . Disability rights groups argue that the disabled still face discrimination and a lack of concerted action . <h> Universal credit and minimum wage <h> Conservatives <p> The party is committed to continue the roll-out of the controversial six-in-one benefit and pledges to do more to ensure that it works " for the most vulnerable " as well as supporting the main carer in every family . The age limit for the National Living Wage will be lowered to 21 ( currently 25 ) and reach ? 10.39 per hour by 2024 . <p> Labour <p> Jeremy Corbyn has pledged to scrap Universal Credit and replace the Department for Work and Pensions with a new Department for Social Security . It promises an alternative benefits system that " treats people with dignity and respect " , including scrapping work capability assessments . It wants to introduce a minimum standard of living . The minimum wage will be increased to ? 10 per hour as a Real Living Wage for all employees aged 16 and over by 2020 . <p> Liberal Democrats <p> Universal Credit will be reformed rather than scrapped . The maximum wait for first payments will reduced from five weeks to five days and the two-child limit will be abolished . The sanctions regime will be replaced with an " incentive-based scheme " . People on zero-hours contracts will receive a 20 per cent higher minimum wage to compensate for the uncertainty of fluctuating hours of work <p> Green Party <p> A Universal Basic Income ( UBI ) will replace Universal Credit by 2025 . This will provide a weekly payment of ? 89 for everybody -- including the employed -- and replace the current benefits system . Added income would be available for groups such as the disabled and single parents . Workers on zero-hours contracts would receive at least the minimum wage and the UBI will be worth at least up to 15 per cent than the minimum wage for those working 37.5 hours per week . <p> Brexit Party <p> The party states that Universal Credit " needs to be revisited " and it will undertake a 12-month review with reforms to follow within two years . Its election " contract " makes no mention of the minimum wage . <p> UKIP <p> The party states that Universal Credit is based on " good principles " including " ending incentives to stay unemployed " . But it says the benefit should not be implemented in a way that causes " unnecessary hardship " . It will seek to limit the use of zero-hours contracts to ensure " everyone can earn a living wage " . <h> SNP <p> The party says Universal Credit is causing " real hardship " and should be radically reformed by scrapping the two-child cap on child tax credits and the " appalling rape clause " . Powers over the minimum wage are reserved to Westminster , but the party 's manifesto calls for employment law to be devolved to Scotland so it can increase the living wage . <p> Plaid Cymru <p> The party pledges to take control of Universal Credit in Wales to reverse the effects of " a decade of austerity " . It opposes the use of zero-hours contracts and seeks a " real living wage " for those working in the public sector or for private companies servicing the public sector . <p> Summary : <p> With the predictable exception of the Conservatives , all parties are pledged to either scrapping or reforming Universal Credit . The Greens have arguably the most radical policy of introducing a guaranteed single income to replace existing benefits . <h> Flexible working , four-day week <h> Conservatives <p> The party will consult on making flexible working a " default " unless employers can put forward good reasons why it is not suitable . Employees will also have the right to demand a " predictable contract " . Party leader Boris Johnson has described Labour 's idea of a four-day week as a " crackpot plan " . <p> Labour <p> An entitlement to flexible working will mean every employee would have the right to choose the pattern of their working hours from their first day in a job . Employers would also be obliged to have a menopause policy , including flexible working , for all women . The party aims to introduce a 32-hour full-time working week within a decade , though this could vary by sector . Think-tanks have put the cost of the four-day week at between ? 3bn and ? 17bn . <p> Liberal Democrats <p> Flexible working will be available to all employees from day one of employment unless employers can put forward a strong case why that should not apply . Agency workers will have the right to a fixed-hours contract after 12 months of employment . <p> Green Party <p> Under a " quality of life guarantee " , people will have a right to flexible hours , in particular those with young children to ensure those who wish to return to work can do so . The party will " support employers to explore four day working weeks " with the aim of increasing productivity and boosting the wellbeing of staff . <p> Brexit Party <p> The party states that leaving the European Union will free the UK from rules such as restrictions on state aid to create thousands of new jobs in strategic industries . It makes no specific pledges on flexible working or the length of the working week . <p> UKIP <p> The party states that " on leaving the EU , UKIP will protect workers ' rights " . It makes no specific pledges on flexible working or the length of the working week . <h> SNP <p> Strongly supports flexible working . The SNP-led Scottish Government has commissioned a feasibility study for a " Centre for Flexible Work " to design and test new approaches in this area . A motion calling for the party to examine the possibility of a four-day week was submitted to the party 's spring conference this year , but it did not make it onto the final agenda . <p> Plaid Cymru <p> The party says it supports the right of workers to seek flexible working arrangements , particularly women and those with young families . It has pointed out that a lower proportion of employers offer flexible working in Wales than in England and Scotland . <p> Summary : <p> Flexible working is a buzzword in many party manifestos , often presented as part of a package to reform the modern workplace . Only two parties have formally expressed a desire to shorten the working week . <h> Parental rights -- childcare <h> Conservatives <p> The party will invest in " wraparound childcare " , meaning provision will be increased for after school and during holidays as part of a ? 1bn fund to create more " high-quality and affordable " childcare and ensure parents do not have to choose between family and their careers . <p> Labour <p> A package worth ? 4.5bn will be spent on opening 1,000 new early years Sure Start centres and extending the entitlement to 30 hours of free childcare to all children between two and four . The party says it wants to see the early years sector move towards a " qualified , graduate-led workforce " and improve the pay and skills of childcare workers . <p> Liberal Democrats <p> A total of 35 hours free childcare will be available to working families from the age of nine months as part of a ? 14.6bn " investment in the country 's future " . All children aged two to four will be eligible for 35 hours of funded childcare for 48 weeks a year , regardless of their parents ' working status . <p> Green Party <p> A total of 35 hours per week of free childcare for all children from the age of nine months . This will include workplace creches to allows parents greater flexibility with returning to work . The measure is part of an ? 86.2bn " green new deal " . <p> Brexit Party <p> The party pledges to invest in education and expanding parental choice . It makes no specific pledges on childcare or early years funding . <p> UKIP <p> The party is opposed to free universal childcare for three and four-year-olds , arguing the policy is poorly targeted and has led to distorted prices . It will scrap universal provision and instead target childcare subsidies towards the most disadvantaged families . Business rates on childcare centres will also be reduced to zero . <p> SNP <p> Pressure UK ministers to increase maternity leave to a year and set maternity pay at 100 per cent of average weekly earnings for the first 12 weeks , then 90 per cent for 40 weeks or ? 150 , whichever is lower . In Scotland , the Sure Start grant has been replaced with a new expanded payment giving eligible families ? 600 on the birth of their first child and ? 300 on the birth of any subsequent children . <p> Plaid Cymru <p> The party will offer universal free childcare for 40 hours per week across Wales . It will also introduce a new ? 35 per week payment for every child in low-income families to tackle child poverty . <p> Summary : <p> There is clear movement towards more state-funded childcare in the early years . Much of this is presented as part of a package to help young families and encourage a return to work . <h> Industrial relations <h> Conservatives <p> A single enforcement body will be created to " crackdown " on any employers abusing employment law , for example taking tips or refusing sick pay . There will be a requirement for a " minimal service " during transport strikes , though it is not explained how this would work . <p> Labour <p> The party will remove " unnecessary restrictions " on industrial action while also enforcing the right of trade unions to enter workplaces . Protections for trade union representatives will be increased and the law around union recognition will be simplified . The party has denied that it will allow the return of secondary picketing but stated it will uphold the right of people to withdraw their labour . <p> Liberal Democrats <p> The ability of unions to represent workers " effectively in the modern economy " will be strengthened , including the introduction of a right to access workplaces . A new Worker Protection Enforcement Authority will be set up to safeguard those in " precarious work " . Employees in listed companies with more than 250 staff will have a right to request shares . <p> Green Party <p> The party pledges to " revive the role of deomcratic trade unions " and require employers to recognise any union that their staff have chosen to represent them . Major companies will have a requirement of at least 40 per cent female representation on their boards . <p> Brexit Party <p> Employers will be encouraged to invest in jobs and be involved in training and apprenticeships . Its proposed " contract " with voters does not make specific pledges on industrial relations . <p> UKIP <p> The party pledges to " protect workers ' rights " on leaving the European Union . It will reintroduce so-called " Whitley councils " or joint employer/employee negotiating bodies in the civil service . <p> Plaid Cymru <p> The party states that Brexit is a threat to workers ' rights and will protect or extend those rights with measures including a legal ban on pregnant women being made redundant or until six months after maternity leave . Employment Action Zones will also be established in areas of high joblessness with exemptions from National Insurance for employers . <p> SNP <p> Industrial action is n't specifically mentioned in its manifesto as the law in this area is reserved , but the party 's MPs will press for the devolution of employment law to allow the Scottish Parliament to protect workers ' rights . <p> Summary : <p> The Labour Party , partly funded by unions , puts forward a clear set of reforms to bolster the role of unions . Elsewhere there are pledges to do more to protect employees from unscrupulous employers . <h> Equality <h> Conservatives <p> The party makes several pledges , including an undertaking to " vigorously combat harassment and violence " against all religious groups and the LGBT community . It will set up a Constitution , Rights and Democracy Commission to examine what is the " proper balance " between the rights of the individual , national security and effective government . The party says it will fight health inequality and promote equality of opportunity in schools . <p> Labour <p> There will be a new Department for Women and Equalities with a Cabinet-level minister whose responsibilities will include ensuring all policies and laws are assessed for impact on equality and inequalities . In particular , the party says it will close the gender pay gap by 2030 and extend pay-gap reporting to include ethnic minorities . It will maintain funding to protect places of worship and consult on putting religious community protection groups on a statutory footing . <p> Liberal Democrats <p> The party states that it will defend the Human Rights Act and resist any attempt to withdraw from the European Convention on Human Rights . All hate crimes will be automatically classed as aggravated offences . A gender " X " option will be introduced for passports and equality law will be extended to cover gender identity . LGBT+ status will be included as a question within the 2021 census . <p> Green Party <p> The gender pay gap will be closed with all medium and large companies required to conduct audits and then redress inequalities of pay . The law will be changed to make it easier to take action against employers on this issue . The parental opt-out for children learning about LGBT relationships will be ended . All political parties will be required to report the diversity of their candidates . <p> Brexit Party <p> The party has an over-arching pledge to change British politics " for good " while not itself seeking to form a government . It offers a new power to initiate referendums subject to a threshhold of five million signatures of registered voters . <p> UKIP <p> The party will repeal the Equality Act 2010 , which it says wrongly gives special rights and privileges to groups with " protected characeristics " and instead introduce a law for " general non-discrimination " . It will also disband the Equalities and Human Rights Commission , which its describes as indulging in " Cultural Marxist social engineering of society " . It also opposes any law to make gender a " self-declared condition " . <p> SNP <p> In Scotland , the voluntary Scottish Business Pledge scheme already encourages firms to pay workers the living wage , close the gender pay gap and never use exploitative zero-hours contracts . The party says its MPs will also back moves to increase worker representation on company boards and argue for greater representation of women and minority communities . <p> Plaid Cymru <p> Support for the LGBT community will include a requirement for schools to keep a register of bullying based on sexuality and promotion of participation in sport . A reform of the Equality Act 2010 will introduce the concept of " gender identity " and remove the use of the terms " gender reassignment " and " transsexual " . <p> Summary <p> Parties across the political want to be seen to address equality issues and there is some new thinking on measures to bolster equality measures . Perhaps unsurprisingly , left-leaning parties place more emphasis on ensuring equality across society . <h> Pensioner benefits <h> Conservatives <p> The party will keep the triple lock on the state pension , meaning it will rise in line with whichever is highest of wages , prices or 2.5 per cent . The winter fuel payment , the pensioner bus pass and other benefit will be kept to " ensure that older people have the security and dignity they deserve " . The party believes free TV licences for the over-75s should be kept and paid for by the BBC . <p> Labour <p> The party guarantees that pensioner benefits will be protected , including the Winter Fuel Payment and free bus passes . It will also ensure the restoration of free television licences for the over-75s . The state pension age will remain at 66 and plans to raise it will be abandoned . Retirement ages in physically arduous jobs will be reviewed . The " triple lock " will be maintained on the state pension . <p> Liberal Democrats <p> The triple lock will be retained on the state pension , meaning it will rise in line with whichever is highest of wages , prices or 2.5 per cent . The system of pension tax relief will be reformed . <p> Green Party <p> The party 's Universal Basic Income policy will replace the state pension and pensioner benefits will be maintained , such as free television licences . The UBI will stand at ? 178 per week for all pensioners , regardless of income or savings -- this is ? 10 higher than the current highest state pension level . There will be a supplement for lone pensioners . Pensioners in need of home care in England will receive it for free <p> Brexit Party <p> The party states that providing a safety net is a " defining mark of a civilised society " but makes no specific pledges on pensioner benefits . It states it will review the position of so-called WASPI women born in the 1950s and short-changed by rises in the pension age . <p> UKIP <p> The party will maintain the state pension " triple lock " and pledges a review of the National Insurance system to investigate " higher and more sustainable pensions " . It suggests options include the creation of a Sovereign Wealth Fund to underpin the state pension using the proceeds of the UK 's natural gas reserves . <p> SNP <p> Will fight to reverse cuts to pension credit , which it says could leave older couples in Scotland around ? 7,000 per year worse off , and campaign to keep the BBC licence fee free for over-75s . Its manifesto points out that pension credit has one of the lowest take-ups of any benefit and calls for a national awareness campaign to ensure it is paid out to the maximum number of people . <p> Plaid Cymru <p> Pensioner benefits will be maintained , along with the state pension " triple lock " . The free bus pass will therefore remain and the BBC will be required to reverse the cuts to the free television licence . The party will also support keeping public toilets open in town centres and other locations so older people can maintain their independence . <p> Summary : <p> Most parties are careful to emphasise the continuation of existing pensioner benefits and assurances about the level of the state pension . No votes are won by pledging to reduce safeguards for the elderly . <h> Britain and the world <h> Security <p> Conservatives <p> 20,000 more police officers on the streets with extra powers to stop and search and target known knife carriers , prevent more foreign national offenders entering the UK , expand role of police and crime commissioners and introduce a new national cyber crime force using new technologies . New law to protest emergency workers from assault , strengthen National Crime Agency , improve safety and security at public venues in wake of 2017 Manchester Arena terror attack and a new Victims ' Law to guarantee victims ' rights . <p> Labour <p> 2,000 more police officers than the Conservatives , extra resources to tackle wildlife crime , new law to protect emergency workers , work to eliminate institutional bias against black and ethnic minority communities , improve police training on domestic abuse and overhaul cyber security . On terrorism , ensure closer coordination between police and security services , and review the Prevent counter-radicalisation programme to safeguard those vulnerable to recruitment propaganda . <p> Liberal Democrats <p> Adopt a " public health approach to serious violence " with ? 500m to restore youth services and ? 1bn for community policing , enough for two new police officers in every ward , with cooperation from teachers , health professionals and youth workers to stop young people falling into gangs . Introduce youth intervention specialists in all major trauma centres , more funding for the National Crime Agency , end disproportionate use of stop and search and more funding to tackle domestic abuse and support victims . <p> Green Party <p> Invest in youth services to deter young people from getting into gangs , more funding for community policing including more liaison and equality officers to work on improving relations with local communities . Make misogyny a hate crime and increase resources for police to deal with domestic violence . <p> Brexit Party <p> Withdrawal from the EU with a " clean-break Brexit " to control the UK 's own national security and borders . Increase police numbers and fund more visible policing with a focus on combating violent crime , robbery and burglary as a priority over enforcing restrictions on free speech . Target county lines drug dealers , gangs and the growth of knife crime . <p> Plaid Cymru <p> Would phase in an increase in spending on foreign aid from 0.7 per cent to 1 per cent of our gross national income ( GNI ) , making us the third highest donor , by that measure , in the world by 2021 . Ensure that all UK aid is aimed at the poorest , and is locally designed , appropriate and subject to local scrutiny . Where feasible , aid will be given as grants , not loans . <h> Defence <p> Conservatives <p> Pledges to continue meeting Nato 's target of spending two per cent of GDP on defence and promises increases of at least 0.5 per cent above inflation every year . Would maintain the Trident nuclear missile system and build the new Type 31 frigates in shipyards such as Rosyth and a new generation of armoured vehicles . Would increase investment in cybersecurity . <p> Labour <p> Would maintain Britain 's commitment to Nato and spend at least two per cent of GDP on defence . Promising to use the UK 's commitment at the United Nations to " support peace and security worldwide " , would increase funding for UN peacekeeping operations to ? 100m . Armed forces pay would be boosted by scrapping the public sector pay cap . <p> Liberal Democrats <p> Committed to spending two per cent of GDP on defence in line with Nato stipulations . Say they would maintain a " minimum nuclear deterrent " while pursuing multilateral nuclear disarmament and press ahead with the Dreadnought submarine programme . Pledge to address skills shortages by giving ? 10,000 " golden handshakes ' to graduates who become armed forces engineers . <p> Green Party <p> The Ministry of Defence would be replaced by a Ministry for Security and Peace and subsidies for arms manufacturers would be scrapped . <p> Brexit Party <p> The UK would spend an " absolute minimum " of two per cent of GDP on defence . By leaving the European Defence Union , the UK would have the right to stipulate defence contracts remain in the UK . Would invest in defence industry , creating thousands of jobs . <p> Plaid Cymru <p> Is demanding a vote of approval in the Welsh Assembly before the UK is involved in foreign wars . Committed to providing " excellent " healthcare to veterans and " adequate " housing for former service personnel . <h> Prisons <p> Conservatives <p> Has made the criminal justice system a central policy following the London Bridge attack . It has pledged to add 10,000 more prison places using ? 2.75bn to refurbish existing prisons . Promised to bring in " tougher " sentencing for the worst offenders and to end automatic halfway release from prison for those convicted of terror-related crimes . Experts have said such measures have already been taken . Will use Brexit to cut number of foreign nationals in UK prisons . <p> Labour <p> Will restore total prison officer numbers to 2010 levels and ensure no prison staff work alone . Pledged to bring PFI prisons back under government ownership and vowed to stop creation of private prisons . Will introduce a presumption against prison sentences of six months or less for non-violent and non-sexual offences . Jeremy Corbyn said those convicted of terrorism offences should " not necessarily " serve full sentence . <p> Liberal Democrats <p> Would recruit 2,000 more prison staff to help with rehabilitation of prisoners . Will introduce a presumption against short sentences and end prison terms for those possessing drugs for personal use . Promises to improve probation services and boost mental health treatment in the criminal justice system . <p> Green Party <p> Vows to halve the prison population by following policies introduced by the Netherlands and will expand restorative justice programmes to replace shorter jail terms , which the party believes have a better record of preventing reoffending . <h> Brexit Party <p> The party is light on reforms to the criminal justice system . Its political " contract with the people " says the party will introduce sentence " ranges " for young offenders to " encourage rehabilitation " . Party leader Nigel Farage said during the campaign convicted terrorists should not be released from prison . <p> Plaid Cymru <p> Is opposed to the building of large-scale " super prisons " in Wales , and aims to cut the proportionally high prisoner numbers in Wales by scrapping short-term sentences , particularly for women . Will use suspended sentences for women charged with non-violent crimes and support dedicated , small , prison or secure centres for female prisoners in Wales . <h> Special relationship <p> Conservatives <p> Boris Johnson has sought to ally himself with Donald Trump and will prioritise getting a trade deal with the US within three years . But the Tories are adamant they will walk away from trade negotiations rather than compromise the UK 's existing animal welfare standards or open up the NHS to privatisation by American firms . <p> Labour <p> The party is strongly opposed to what it calls " the outsourcing of UK foreign policy to US President Donald Trump " , suggesting Jeremy Corbyn would break with decades of precedent to distance the UK from America on the international stage . He has also promised to pressure Mr Trump to take more action on climate change . <p> Liberal Democrats <p> The party 's manifesto says : " President Trump has repeatedly acted to cause instability , whether by initiating trade wars or abandoning Kurdish allies in Syria . " The Lib Dems would prioritise working through multilateral bodies such as the UN over the bilateral relationship between Britain and America . <p> Green Party <p> The Greens want to strengthen the UN as a forum for protecting the climate , rather than focussing on traditional state-to-state diplomacy . A number of their policies , such as declaring the whole of the Arctic a " world nature reserve " which can not be developed , would set up a clash with the US . The Greens ' strict conditions for striking trade deals would rule out any realistic transatlantic agreement . <p> Brexit Party <p> Nigel Farage is a long-standing friend of Mr Trump and is enthusiastic about the possibility of a trade deal between Britain and the US after Brexit . He has dismissed the suggestion the NHS could be damaged by any free-trade agreement . <p> SNP <p> Despite Donald Trump 's close ties to Scotland , including his business interests , SNP ministers have been quick to attack the US President over his views on immigration and human rights . The party 's manifesto also warns of a " real risk " that a post-Brexit UK-US trade deal will open up the NHS to multinational health firms and proposes a new law to stop this from happening . <p> Plaid Cymru <p> Plaid supports several policies including scrapping nuclear weapons which would be opposed by the US government . The party also says : " In the event of leaving the EU , we will strongly oppose the inclusion of the Welsh NHS within any future trade deals with the USA . " <p> Ukip <p> Ukip says Britain " should not allow ourselves to be swept into war on someone else 's coattails " in a suggestion the party would resist joining the US in future military action . <p> In summary <p> Only the Tories and the Brexit Party are enthusiastic about working with the USA under the current Trump administration . Other parties say they would stand up to the President while a Labour government would usher in a totally new era in transatlantic relations . <h> China/Russia <p> Conservatives <p> Boris Johnson wants a post-Brexit trade deal with China but has not put a timeframe on it . He is keen for the country to end its trade war with the US . The Conservatives say that Russia should be held to account for " destabilising activity " in other countries , such as election manipulation and targeted assassinations , but have so far refused to release a parliamentary report into its behaviour . <p> Labour <p> Labour has demanded the instant release of the report into alleged Russian meddling in British elections . Jeremy Corbyn has denied benefiting from Russian hacking himself , after the leak of a document describing US-UK trade talks . He has said Britain should do more to hold China to account over its human-rights record . <p> Liberal Democrats <p> The UK government should support Ukraine in its struggle to shake off Russian domination , and challenge Vladimir Putin for " persistently threatening the international rules-based order " . Jo Swinson has previously praised China 's government as a " voice of reason " in international relations , but the party criticises the regime 's treatment of the Uighur people . <p> Green Party <p> The Greens want to work with China and other large developing countries to ensure their economic growth does not result in environmental destruction . It has called for tougher action on allies of Putin who are able to stash their money in the UK without being held to account for how they came by it . <p> Brexit Party <p> Sceptical of claims Russia has interfered in British elections , calling them " baseless propaganda and scare stories used to shut down debate " . Nigel Farage has demanded greater curbs on the import of cheap steel from China , claiming it has harmed the industry in the UK . <p> SNP <p> Foreign policy is reserved to Westminster , but with Chinese tourism booming in Scotland , SNP ministers have promoted the economic ties and cultural links between the two countries . On Russia , the party 's defence spokesman Stewart McDonald has been a vocal critic of Vladimir Putin , hitting out at the " heavy fist " of the Kremlin in dealing with its neighbours . <p> Plaid Cymru <p> MPs from Plaid Cymru have demanded that the UK government stand up to China on the issue of Tibet . The party cast doubt on the evidence Vladimir Putin 's government was responsible for the nerve agent attack on Salisbury last year . <p> Ukip <p> In the past senior Ukip figures have repeatedly been accused of links to Russia -- but also claim to have been targeted by Russian meddling designed to suppress their vote . Some from the party have warned against a new trade deal with China . <p> In summary <p> None of the parties has set out a detailed blueprint to deal with either Russia or China , the two global superpowers with which Britain has the most complex relationship . They are united in opposition to Vladimir Putin 's behaviour but divided on whether or not it is damaging British democracy . On China , most parties support close engagement but they are wary of being bound too tightly to the country . <h> Trident and Nato <p> Conservatives <p> We will continue to exceed the NATO target of spending 2 per cent of GDP on defence and increase the budget by at least 0.5 per cent above inflation every year of the new Parliament . We will maintain our Trident nuclear deterrent , which guarantees our security . And we will adapt to new threats , investing more in cybersecurity and setting up the UK 's first Space Command . We will stand against terrorism and extremism around the world . After Brexit , we will bolster the alliances and institutions that help project our influence and keep us safe , such as the UN and the UN Security Council and NATO . <p> Labour <p> Will increase funding for UN peacekeeping operations to ? 100 million . and maintain the UK 's commitment to NATO and close relationship with Europe . Will use the country 's influence at the United Nations to support peace and security worldwide . Supports the renewal of the Trident nuclear deterrent and will actively lead multilateral efforts under our obligations to the Non-Proliferation Treaty to create a nuclear-free world <p> Liberal Democrats <p> Commit to the principle of collective self-defence as laid out in the North Atlantic Treaty and spending two per cent of GDP on defence in line with NATO recommendations.The Lib Dems do n't mention but promise to " maintain a minimum nuclear deterrent , while pursuing multilateral nuclear disarmament . <p> Green Party <p> Would cancel the Trident weapons system and nuclear-powered submarines and work to eliminate nuclear weapons worldwide . Cash saved from scrapping Trident would be used for developing non-carbon emitting technology . <p> Brexit Party <p> There is no mention of Trident . Nigel Farage 's party would ensure that the UK maintains its commitment to NATO . <p> SNP <p> Strongly against the renewal of Trident and wants the nuclear submarines to be removed permanently from Scotland , describing them as " immoral , ineffective and expensive " . Nicola Sturgeon has said this would be a " red line " in any talks with Labour after the election . The party is currently in favour of Nato membership -- provided that Trident is removed from Scotland . <p> Plaid Cymru <p> Plaid Cymru has consistently opposed what it calls the hugely wasteful and dangerous replacement of Trident , which is expected to cost at least ? 205 billion . It would scrap the scheme and spend the money on public services and infrastructure . Would oppose attempts to site nuclear weapons in Wales or Welsh waters . The manifesto does n't mention Nato . <h> Overseas Aid <p> Conservatives <p> After Brexit , will bolster the alliances and institutions that help boost trade such as the Commonwealth ; the G20 ; the G7 ; and the World Trade Organisation . " We will open new markets and support free trade and global growth . " <p> Labour <p> Will end ' bomb first , talk later ' approach and instead have a foreign policy based on peace , justice and human rights . Will immediately suspend the sale of arms to Saudi Arabia for use in Yemen and to Israel for arms used in violation of the human rights of Palestinian civilians . Will conduct a root-and-branch reform of arms exports regime . <p> Liberal Democrats <p> We commit to spending 0.7 per cent of Gross National Income on aid . This would be spent reducing poverty , defending human rights , protecting the environment and preventing violent conflict worldwide . We would also work to controlling arms exports to countries with poor human rights records and , as part of this , suspend arms sales to Saudi Arabia . Would promote democracy and stability in Ukraine and neighbouring countries against an increasingly aggressive Russia . <p> Green Party <p> Would phase in an increase in spending on foreign aid from 0.7 per cent to 1 per cent of our gross national income ( GNI ) , making us the third highest donor , by that measure , in the world by 2021 . Ensure that all UK aid is aimed at the poorest , and is locally designed , appropriate and subject to local scrutiny . Where feasible , aid will be given as grants , not loans . <p> Brexit Party <p> The party would cut the foreign aid budget in half , saving ? 40bn over the five-year term and spend the money to boost UK services instead . Pledges to stop the tragedy associated with human trafficking . <p> Plaid Cymru <p> The party wants Wales to be a nation of sanctuary for refugees fleeing war and oppression and will help refugees and asylum seekers integrate into Welsh society . Future trade deals taken by the UK , whether inside or outside the EU , should maintain and enhance environmental standards , minimise the environmental footprint of trade and make trade terms explicitly subject to environmental and human rights commitments .

@@42065532 <h> Nikhil Rathi Appointed As New Chief Executive Of The FCA <p> Date 22/06/2020 <p> HM Treasury have today announced the appointment of Nikhil Rathi as the new permanent Chief Executive of the Financial Conduct Authority ( FCA ) . <p> Nikhil is currently the Chief Executive of London Stock Exchange plc . From September 2009 to April 2014 , he was Director , Financial Services Group at HM Treasury . In this role , he led the Treasurys work on the UKs EU and international financial services interests . ( But it probably does n't . ) <p> The study , published in the Scientific Reports journal , aimed to demonstrate that assessments of emissions associated with different forms of travel should take into account emissions associated with that person possibly eating more in response to their increased physical activity . <p> While conceding that , " studies of active transport do not currently provide us with definitive information on the extent or nature of compensatory food intake in response to increased walking and cycling , " researchers assume that a person who shifts from a passive mode of transport ( e.g. driving ) will eat a little more . <p> They base their calculations @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 2010 book , The Carbon Footprint of Everything . @@42070523 <h> Carpe Diem ! How the philosophy of ' seize the day ' was hijacked and what the phrase should mean <h> Carpe diem , meaning ' seize the day , ' is one of the most powerful philosophical ideals . Now it 's used to sell trainers , T-shirts ... <p> The flagship store of Nike in Shanghai markets the spirit of carpe diem to shoppers ( Photo : JOHANNES EISELE/AFP/Getty Images ) <h> Carpe diem , meaning ' seize the day , ' is one of the most powerful philosophical ideals . Now it 's used to sell trainers , T-shirts and a carefree lifestyle ( #YOLO ) . But Roman Krznaric wonders if we 're getting the message <p> On a summer 's morning in 2014 , 89-year-old Bernard Jordan decided to escape . The former British naval officer was determined to go to Normandy to celebrate the 70th anniversary of the D-Day landings with other veterans . But there was a problem : he was trapped in a care home in Hove , without permission to travel . What could he do ? <p> Bernard came up with a cunning plan . He got up @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to pin on his wartime medals , then covered his outfit with a grey raincoat and sneaked out of the home . Now free , he tottered down to the railway station nearly a mile away , and took the train to Portsmouth . Once there , he boarded the ferry to France and joined a party of war veterans who took him under their wing . <p> As soon as the care staff realised he was missing , a frantic police search began . But it was too late . Bernard was already across the Channel , surrounded by marching bands and dancing girls . " I loved every minute of it and would do it again tomorrow -- it was such an exciting experience , " he said on his return . " I expect I will be in some trouble with the care home , but it was worth it . " <h> The i newsletter cut through the noise <p> Email address is invalidEmail address is invalid <p> Thank you for subscribing ! <p> Sorry , there was a problem with your subscription . <p> The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ by storm , knocking the sober anniversary speeches by world leaders off the front pages . The ferry company even offered him free travel to Normandy for the rest of his life . But Bernard was never able to take up that offer : six months later , he died . <p> Why did Bernard 's adventure capture so much public attention ? It was not just nostalgia for the wartime spirit or his venerable age . People also admired his courage to seize a window of opportunity . The chance was there , and he took it . As one person commented in an online forum just after his death : " RIP , am doubly glad he escaped and got to go to the anniversary ... carpe diem . " <p> Bernard Jordan waves as he returns to Portsmouth on a Brittany Ferry <h> Not just any old saying <p> Carpe diem -- seize the day -- is one of the most powerful philosophical ideals to have emerged in Western history . First uttered by the Roman poet Horace over 2,000 years ago , it retains an extraordinary @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Metallica have rocked audiences around the world with their song " Carpe Diem Baby " , while the actress Dame Judi Dench had " CARPE DIEM " tattooed on her wrist for her 81st birthday . It 's a message found in films such as Dead Poets Society , in one of the most successful brand campaigns of the last century ( " Just Do It " ) , and in social media #yolo ( you only live once ) . <p> You can even get T-shirts with the slogan " CARPE THAT F****NG DIEM " . <p> Metallica encourage their fans to live for the moment during their gigs ( Photo : Mauricio Santana/Getty Images ) <p> The message of carpe diem matters more than ever today . We live in an age of distraction , where we are checking our phones , on average , 110 times a day , and are more interested in being spectators of life on the screen than living it for ourselves . Immersed in the second-hand pleasures offered by our electronic gadgets , we need to reconnect with the wisdom of carpe @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the wonders of experiential living in the short time we have before death . <p> The challenge , however , is that many of us are losing touch with the deep carpe diem drive that has motivated people such as Bernard Jordan . The possibilities of radical aliveness are slipping away from us . The reason ? Carpe diem has been hijacked . It 's the existential crime of the century -- and one that we have barely noticed . Who , or what , are the hijackers ? <p> Roman satirist and poet Horace ( Photo : Hulton Archive/Getty Images ) <h> How the phrase was seized <p> First , the spirit of " seize the day " has been surreptitiously hijacked by consumer culture , which has recast it as Black Friday shopping sprees and the instant hit of one-click online buying -- Just Do It has come to mean just buy it . <p> Alongside this is the growing cult of efficiency and time management that has driven us toward hyper-scheduled living , turning the spontaneity of Just Do It into a culture of just plan it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ -- carpe diem has been hijacked by the booming mindfulness movement . While practising mindfulness has many proven benefits , from reducing stress to helping with depression , one of its unintended consequences has been to encourage the narrow idea that seizing the day is primarily about living in the here and now . Just Do It has become " just breathe " . The popularity of " present moment awareness " -- which is so attractive in an age where we are busy doing rather than being -- is crowding out the variety of ways that human beings have discovered over the centuries to seize the day . <p> Confronted by these hijackers , we need to rediscover five approaches to seizing the day that have emerged since the days of Horace as an antidote to our awareness -- often fleeting -- that our time is running out . <h> Once in a lifetime <p> The most popular form of seizing the day I call opportunity -- it 's about following Bernard Jordan 's example and taking windows of opportunity that may never be repeated , whether it 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ rescue a crumbling relationship . <p> It 's worth knowing that the word " opportunity " comes from the Latin ob portum veniens , meaning " coming toward a port " . It originally referred to a favourable wind that would blow a ship into harbour . So the question is whether we 're going to hoist our sails and catch this propitious wind , or whether we are so worried about hitting the rocks that we keep the sails down . <p> A second strategy is hedonism , where we seize the day through sensory pleasures , from free love to gastronomic exploration . Hedonism has an admittedly bad reputation , being associated with binge drinking and Trainspotting-style heroin overdoses . But do n't forget that hedonism -- in healthy doses -- has been a route to human wellbeing for millennia : when the conquistadors arrived in the Americas , they discovered the Aztecs tripping on magic mushrooms . Downing a few tequila slammers or smoking a joint under the stars can sometimes help us with our troubles just as much as a trip to a therapist . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ carpe diem is presence , which is about stepping into the now . Mindfulness meditation is one way of doing this , but there are other options such as what psychologists call " flow experience " . This is where you engage in a challenging and often vigorous activity that completely absorbs you in the present moment , like a high-speed basketball game . You 're utterly " in the zone " . Entering the now through the intense rush of sports is quite different from doing so by practising breathing techniques . <p> Fourth is spontaneity , which involves throwing plans and routines to the wind and becoming more experimental in the way we live . We need to liberate ourselves from our electronic calendars and booking up our weekends weeks in advance , and recover a more unplanned approach to the art of living which existed before the Industrial Revolution , when we were n't constantly checking the time and obsessed with being " efficient " and " productive " . <p> Finally , we need to rediscover political carpe diem . This is about taking the four @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , presence and spontaneity -- and ratcheting them up from the individual to the collective level through mass political action . Think of the carpe diem demonstrations that brought down the Berlin Wall in 1989 , which were full of spontaneous and hedonistic spirit . We need more of this today to challenge the big issues of our time , from climate change to the rise of far-right extremism . <p> Look at your own life and you may see an abundance of these five approaches to seizing the day . But you might also notice a deficit in one or more of them . Now is the moment to look away from the screen and embrace a life inspired by those two words : carpe diem .

@@42073346 <h> PETER TRUDGILL on the ultimate origins of ' English ' . <p> Almost four years after its creation The New European goes from strength to strength across print and online , offering a pro-European perspective on Brexit and reporting on the political response to the coronavirus outbreak , climate change and international politics . But we can only continue to grow with your support . <p> During the late 300s and early 400s AD , boat-loads of Germanic people started crossing the North Sea to the eastern shores of Britain . Some arrivals had probably come well before that : since the second century AD , the Romans had been employing Germanic mercenaries in their garrisons in Britain . <p> These Germanic people were mostly members of the tribal groupings we now refer to as the Jutes , Angles , Saxons , and Frisians . They came mainly from coastal districts just across the North Sea from Britain . <p> The Jutes had originally come from the furthest north , from northern and central Jutland , now part of Denmark . The Angles lived in areas to the south of them in southern Jutland and Schleswig-Holstein . The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the North Sea coastal areas of northern Germany in the Elbe-Weser region of Saxony . And the Frisians came from Friesland , the area of coastline between the homeland of the Saxons and the mouth of the River Rhine in the modern Netherlands . <p> The great estuaries of the English East Coast -- such as the Humber , the Wash , the estuary of the Stour and the Orwell at Harwich , and the Thames Estuary -- formed major entry points into Britain for many of these people . <h> You may also want to watch : <p> Of these Germanic peoples , it was the Saxons who eventually gave their name to the areas of southern England known as Wessex , Sussex , Middlesex and Essex , the names referring respectively to the West , South , Middle and East Saxons . <p> In these Saxon-dominated areas of England , we do find a few toponyms which indicate rather clearly that most people in Wessex were not Angles , such as the Wessex settlement of Englefield , now in Berkshire , which meant the ' field of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Angles ' , in Devon . <p> There were also Frisians around , as we can see from the Suffolk village names Friston and Freston , ' homestead of the Frisians ' , as well as from the name of Frisby in Leicestershire . But most of non-Saxon England and southeastern Scotland came to be dominated by Angles . <p> In these Anglian zones , there are still to this day village names such as Saxham ' home of the Saxons ' , near Bury St Edmunds , and Saxton ' homestead of the Saxons ' , in North Yorkshire : these villages were obviously so called because there was something unusual about being a Saxon in Suffolk and Yorkshire . <p> The Saxons , then , gave their name to Essex and Middlesex and Sussex , but it was the Angles who had the honour of eventually giving their name to England , ' the land of the Angles ' , and to the English language . But why were they called Angles ? <p> We first hear about them from the Roman historian Tacitus ( c. 56-120 AD @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . They seem to have come originally from the area of Germany which is now known as Angeln . This is a peninsula which is on the eastern coast of the Schleswig-Holstein , on the Baltic Sea . Angeln lies between the Flensburg Firth , which today forms part of the border between Denmark and Germany , and the Schlei Inlet , which leads from the Baltic Sea to the town of Schleswig . Almost everybody from the Angeln area seems to have emigrated to Britain in the 5th century AD . <p> As to why Angeln is called Angeln , there are different theories . It could be derived from the word which has come down into modern German as eng , ' narrow ' , referring perhaps to the narrow waters of the Schlei Inlet . Or it could be related to angle , ' bend , corner ' . Or to angling as in fishing . Angle in the fishing sense originally referred to the bent or angled implement fishermen use for catching fish on a line .
